title: From the Dungeon to Pharaoh’s Right Hand
summary: God gives Pharaoh two dreams that only Joseph can interpret; the forgotten prisoner is made ruler of Egypt and stores grain that saves many nations.
historicalContext: Two more years pass after the cupbearer forgets Joseph, who is now thirty and has spent thirteen years as a slave and prisoner (37:2; 41:46). Egypt’s life hung on the yearly flood of the Nile: a low river meant failed harvests, and records from several periods speak of long famines and of officials who boasted of feeding the hungry. Pharaoh’s magicians were lector priests trained in sacred writings, spells, and dream books, so their failure is a defeat for the whole learning of Egypt. The details of Joseph’s promotion fit Egyptian court practice closely: shaving before an audience, the royal seal, linen garments, the gold collar of honour, a chariot, a herald’s cry, an Egyptian name, and marriage into the priestly family of On, the centre of sun worship. A vizier with this sweep of authority suits the period before the New Kingdom, possibly when Semitic rulers held power in the Delta.
literaryContext: Genesis 41 is the turning point of the Joseph story. The man forgotten at the end of chapter 40 is remembered, raised, and given authority over a third house, now Pharaoh’s, after Potiphar’s and the prison keeper’s (39:4, 22). The chapter moves from dreams (vv. 1-8) to remembrance (vv. 9-13), to an audience in which Pharaoh retells what the reader already knows (vv. 14-24), to God’s interpretation and Joseph’s counsel (vv. 25-36), to installation (vv. 37-46), and finally to seven years of plenty and the onset of famine (vv. 47-57). Things come in pairs throughout: two years, two dreams, two sevens, two sons. God is named again and again in Joseph’s speech, so that the king of Egypt hears that heaven governs his river. The closing note that all countries came to Egypt for grain sets the stage for the arrival of Joseph’s brothers in chapter 42.
themes: God’s sovereign rule over nations and nature
Revelation given by God, not human skill
The Spirit of God and practical wisdom
Faithful stewardship in seasons of plenty
Blessing to the nations through Abraham’s seed

outline.title: Pharaoh’s Troubled Dreams
outline.summary: Pharaoh dreams of lean cows devouring fat ones and thin ears swallowing full ones, and none of Egypt’s magicians or wise men can interpret them.

outline.title: Joseph Summoned from the Dungeon
outline.summary: The cupbearer remembers the young Hebrew who interpreted dreams in prison; Joseph is rushed before Pharaoh and declares that the answer belongs to God alone.

outline.title: The Dream Explained and the Plan Proposed
outline.summary: Pharaoh retells his dreams; Joseph explains that God is announcing seven years of plenty followed by seven of famine and counsels storing a fifth of the harvest under a wise overseer.

outline.title: Joseph Exalted over Egypt
outline.summary: Recognising the Spirit of God in Joseph, Pharaoh makes him ruler over all the land, invests him with ring, linen, chain, and chariot, and gives him a new name and a wife.

outline.title: Plenty, Sons, and Famine
outline.summary: Joseph gathers grain beyond counting, names his sons Manasseh and Ephraim in praise of God, and opens the storehouses to Egypt and the world when the famine comes.

verses.bibleText: And it came to pass at the end of two full years, that Pharaoh dreamed: and, behold, he stood by the river.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Chapter 40 closed with a single bleak line: the chief butler “forgat him.” Chapter 41 opens by measuring how long that forgetting lasted. “At the end of two full years” is literally “at the end of two years of days,” an expression that stresses complete, counted time. For Joseph these were not empty years on a calendar but seven hundred mornings in the same prison, after a hope had flared and died. Added to the eleven years already spent as a slave and prisoner, they bring him to the age of thirty (v. 46).

The narrator does not tell us what Joseph felt. He tells us what God did. Deliverance came, not when the cupbearer finally felt a pang of conscience, but when “Pharaoh dreamed.” The king of Egypt, supposedly the son of the sun god and the guarantor of order in the land, is shown asleep and unable to control what passes through his mind. The God of Joseph speaks to him, as he had earlier spoken by dreams to Abimelech and Laban (20:3; 31:24), and as he would later speak to Nebuchadnezzar (Daniel 2:1). Proverbs states the principle: “The king’s heart is in the hand of the LORD” (Proverbs 21:1).

In the dream Pharaoh “stood by the river.” The word is the ordinary Hebrew term for the Nile, borrowed from Egyptian. Egypt had almost no rain; every harvest and every herd depended on the yearly rise of this one river. Placing Pharaoh on its bank at the start of the dream puts the whole economy and religion of Egypt in view, because the Nile was honoured as the source of life. The God who made the waters (1:9-10) is about to show the king that the river answers to him. Psalm 105 reads the waiting from heaven’s side: “until the time that his word came: the word of the LORD tried him” (Psalm 105:19).

wordNotes.term: מִקֵּץ שְׁנָתַיִם יָמִים (miqqets shenatayim yamim) — at the end of two full years
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “at the end of two years, days.” Adding “days” to a span of time marks it as full and complete, as in Jeremiah’s “two full years” (Jeremiah 28:3). The phrase stresses how long Joseph waited after the cupbearer was restored. The same opening word, miqqets, “at the end of,” marks other turning points that come only when God’s time has run its course (Genesis 8:6; Exodus 12:41).

wordNotes.term: הַיְאֹר (hay’or) — the river
wordNotes.explanation: Ye’or is a loanword from Egyptian and in the Old Testament almost always names the Nile, with its channels and canals (Exodus 1:22; 7:17-21). Only in Daniel 12 does it refer to another river. The choice of this word sets the dream firmly in Egypt and points to the river on which the land’s life depended, the same river later struck in the plagues.

verses.bibleText: And, behold, there came up out of the river seven well favoured kine and fatfleshed; and they fed in a meadow.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The dream begins pleasantly. “Behold,” a word repeated six times in the first seven verses, draws the reader into Pharaoh’s own eyes as he watches. Seven cows climb out of the Nile, “well favoured” and “fatfleshed,” and graze in the reeds along the bank. Cattle in Egypt often stood in the river to escape heat and flies, so the picture is drawn from ordinary life. A herd of fine cows feeding by a full river is exactly what an Egyptian king would hope to see: it means a good flood, rich pasture, and plenty for the land.

Cattle carried weight in Egyptian thought beyond farming. Tomb paintings show rows of cows, and religious texts speak of seven cows that provide food. The dream therefore uses images Pharaoh already understood. God speaks in a language his hearer can grasp, much as he later addressed Nebuchadnezzar through a statue of metals and the wise men from the east through a star (Daniel 2:31-32; Matthew 2:2). Yet the images are not left to Egyptian guesswork. As the chapter will show, their meaning comes only from the God who sent them.

The number seven, prominent throughout Scripture since the seventh day of creation (2:2-3), signals completeness. Here it will mark two complete periods. For the moment the scene is all blessing, and Pharaoh has no reason for alarm. The reader, who knows that dreams in Joseph’s story come in pairs and carry weight, waits for what follows.

wordNotes.term: אָחוּ (achu) — meadow
wordNotes.explanation: Another Egyptian loanword, meaning the reeds or marsh grass that grew along the Nile and its canals. Outside this chapter (vv. 2, 18) it appears only in Job’s question, “Can the flag grow without water?” (Job 8:11). The word paints cattle grazing in the green fringe watered by the river, and the Egyptian vocabulary fits a writer who knew Egypt well.

wordNotes.term: יְפוֹת מַרְאֶה וּבְרִיאֹת בָּשָׂר (yefot mar’eh uveri’ot basar) — well favoured and fatfleshed
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “beautiful of appearance and fat of flesh.” Yefeh, beautiful, is the same word used of Rachel and of Joseph himself (Genesis 29:17; 39:6). Bari’, fat or healthy, describes well-fed animals and people (Judges 3:17; Daniel 1:15). The two terms are carefully reversed for the lean cows in the next verse.

verses.bibleText: And, behold, seven other kine came up after them out of the river, ill favoured and leanfleshed; and stood by the other kine upon the brink of the river.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
A second “behold” turns the dream. Seven more cows rise from the same river, but these are “ill favoured and leanfleshed,” the exact opposite of the first group: ugly instead of beautiful, thin instead of fat. The Hebrew sets the descriptions in mirror image, so that every quality of the first herd is undone in the second. When Pharaoh retells the dream he will add that he had never seen such poor creatures in all Egypt (v. 19).

The detail that disturbs is where these cattle come from. They come “out of the river,” the same source as the fat cows. The Nile, Egypt’s giver of life, is now producing want. For a king whose people believed the flood was governed by the gods and secured by the king’s right relation to them, this was a frightening reversal. The lean cows then “stood by the other kine upon the brink of the river,” side by side with the healthy ones for a moment, as though the years of hunger were already waiting at the edge of the years of plenty.

Scripture often teaches that prosperity and need are both in God’s hand (Deuteronomy 8:17-18; Haggai 1:9-11). Egypt prided itself on a river that rarely failed. The dream gently but firmly removes that confidence. The God of Joseph is about to announce that what comes up out of the Nile in good years and bad comes by his decision.

wordNotes.term: רָעוֹת מַרְאֶה וְדַקּוֹת בָּשָׂר (ra‘ot mar’eh vedaqqot basar) — ill favoured and leanfleshed
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “bad of appearance and thin of flesh.” Ra‘, bad or evil, here describes ugliness rather than moral wickedness, as with the “naughty figs” of Jeremiah 24:2. Daq, thin, is used of the lean cows and then of the thin ears (vv. 6-7), binding the two dreams together. It can describe fine dust or a still small voice (Isaiah 29:5; 1 Kings 19:12), always something slight or wasted.

verses.bibleText: And the ill favoured and leanfleshed kine did eat up the seven well favoured and fat kine. So Pharaoh awoke.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Then the unthinkable happens: “the ill favoured and leanfleshed kine did eat up the seven well favoured and fat kine.” Cows do not eat cows. The image is meant to be unnatural and repulsive, and it carries the message of the dream in a single act. What is weak and wasted swallows what is strong and abundant. The verb is the ordinary word for eating, used of meals throughout Genesis, which makes the scene more grotesque.

The first dream ends abruptly: “So Pharaoh awoke.” He is jolted out of sleep by what he has seen. Genesis records other awakenings after God has spoken in the night, such as Jacob at Bethel and Laban on the road (28:16; 31:24). Pharaoh does not yet know that his dream is a message from God. He knows only that it has troubled him. In verse 21 he will add a detail the narrator holds back here: after eating, the lean cows looked as starved as before, as though they had eaten nothing at all.

The reader may notice a quiet link with Joseph’s life. He had been the favoured son, swallowed up by the jealousy of his brothers and the lies of Potiphar’s wife. Yet the God who allows the lean to devour the fat in Pharaoh’s dream is the same God who will turn Joseph’s losses into the saving of many lives (50:20).

wordNotes.term: וַתֹּאכַלְנָה (vatto’khalnah) — did eat up
wordNotes.explanation: From ’akhal, the everyday verb “to eat.” When animals devour other creatures it often carries a note of violence or judgement, as in the brothers’ lie that “an evil beast hath devoured him” (Genesis 37:20, 33) or the lion that slew the disobedient prophet (1 Kings 13:24). Pharaoh’s retelling will stress that this eating brings the lean cows no gain at all (Genesis 41:21).

verses.bibleText: And he slept and dreamed the second time: and, behold, seven ears of corn came up upon one stalk, rank and good.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Pharaoh falls asleep again “and dreamed the second time.” The scene shifts from the riverbank to the field and from livestock to grain. The two pillars of Egypt’s food supply, herds and harvest, are both brought into view. This time “seven ears of corn came up upon one stalk, rank and good.” “Corn” in the King James Version means grain in general, here probably wheat or barley, not the American maize.

Seven full heads on a single stalk would be an extraordinary sight. A stalk normally bears one ear. The picture is of abundance beyond the ordinary, a harvest so rich that the plant itself seems to overflow. “Rank” is an older English word for full and vigorous growth; the Hebrew is the same word translated “fat” for the cows in verse 2, so the two dreams echo one another word for word. The verb “came up” is also the same verb used for the cows rising from the river.

Repetition is the chief signal of this chapter. Joseph will explain that the dream was doubled because the thing was established by God (v. 32). Joseph himself had dreamed twice, of sheaves and then of stars (37:5-9), and the cupbearer and baker had dreamed on the same night (40:5). God does not stammer when he repeats himself. He repeats to make his message plain and certain. The same principle runs through Scripture: “in the mouth of two or three witnesses shall every word be established” (2 Corinthians 13:1).

wordNotes.term: שִׁבֳּלִים בְּרִיאוֹת וְטֹבוֹת (shibbolim beri’ot vetovot) — ears of corn, rank and good
wordNotes.explanation: Shibbolet is an ear or head of grain, the word later used as a password at the Jordan (Judges 12:6). Beri’ot, fat or plump, repeats the description of the healthy cows (v. 2), and tovot, good, is the familiar word of the creation account (Genesis 1:12). The language ties the two dreams together and presents the first seven as a picture of God’s good provision.

verses.bibleText: And, behold, seven thin ears and blasted with the east wind sprung up after them.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
After the full heads, “seven thin ears and blasted with the east wind sprung up after them.” The east wind in Egypt and Canaan blew in from the desert, hot and dry, and in a few days could shrivel standing grain. Egypt knew it as a seasonal scourge in spring and early autumn. The ears in the dream are not merely small; they have been scorched before they could ripen.

Throughout Scripture the east wind becomes a picture of God’s power to dry up and to judge. Hosea warns that “an east wind shall come, the wind of the LORD shall come up from the wilderness,” and his spring shall become dry (Hosea 13:15). Ezekiel speaks of a vine that withers when the east wind touches it (Ezekiel 17:10). Isaiah observes that grass withers because the breath of the LORD blows upon it (Isaiah 40:7). Yet the same wind serves God’s saving purposes: an east wind drove back the Red Sea so that Israel could cross on dry ground (Exodus 14:21).

In Pharaoh’s dream the scorching wind is the second half of the warning. Whether the cause in the coming years would be a low Nile or drought in neighbouring lands, the images say that the source of famine lies outside Egypt’s control.

wordNotes.term: שְׁדוּפֹת קָדִים (sheduphot qadim) — blasted with the east wind
wordNotes.explanation: Shadaph means to scorch or blight; the participle describes grain withered by heat. Qadim, literally “the front” or “east,” names the dry wind off the desert. The same pairing appears in 2 Kings 19:26, where corn is “blasted before it be grown up.” Elsewhere qadim is the wind God sends to bring locusts or to part the sea (Exodus 10:13; 14:21).

verses.bibleText: And the seven thin ears devoured the seven rank and full ears. And Pharaoh awoke, and, behold, it was a dream.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The second dream ends as the first did, with the weak overwhelming the strong: “the seven thin ears devoured the seven rank and full ears.” The verb changes from “did eat up” to “devoured,” literally “swallowed,” a word used of the earth swallowing Korah or a great fish swallowing Jonah (Numbers 16:32; Jonah 1:17). The full ears simply vanish.

“And Pharaoh awoke, and, behold, it was a dream.” The vividness had been so strong that only on waking did he realise that none of it was physically before him. That final “behold” is the sixth in these verses, and it marks the moment of realisation. Yet the dream does not fade with waking. Its double message stays with him through the remainder of the night and into the morning (v. 8).

Though Pharaoh had two distinct visions, the text soon speaks of them as one “dream” (vv. 8, 15, 25). Both have seven good things followed by seven bad, and both end with the bad consuming the good. Joseph will make that unity the key to their meaning. Here the narrator lets the reader feel what Pharaoh felt before anyone could explain it: a sense that something was coming against which all Egypt’s strength would be swallowed up.

wordNotes.term: וַתִּבְלַעְנָה (vattivla‘nah) — devoured
wordNotes.explanation: From bala‘, to swallow or engulf. It describes something taken in so completely that nothing remains, as when Aaron’s rod swallowed the magicians’ rods (Exodus 7:12) or the earth swallowed Pharaoh’s army (Exodus 15:12). The choice prepares for the explanation that the plenty will be forgotten without trace (Genesis 41:30-31).

verses.bibleText: And it came to pass in the morning that his spirit was troubled; and he sent and called for all the magicians of Egypt, and all the wise men thereof: and Pharaoh told them his dream; but there was none that could interpret them unto Pharaoh.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“In the morning his spirit was troubled.” The Hebrew verb pictures something beating or pounding, like a hammer or a footstep; Pharaoh’s heart is pounding with unease. Nebuchadnezzar later had the same experience after his dream (Daniel 2:1, 3). The repetition of the dream seems to have convinced Pharaoh that it was no ordinary night’s confusion but a message of weight.

He therefore “called for all the magicians of Egypt, and all the wise men thereof.” The magicians were priestly experts trained in sacred writings, ritual spells, and the interpretation of dreams; Egypt had manuals listing dream images with their supposed meanings. The wise men were learned counsellors. Together they represented the full wisdom of the most learned court of the age. Yet “there was none that could interpret them unto Pharaoh.” They may well have offered suggestions, but none satisfied the king. It is worth noticing that Pharaoh speaks of one “dream,” while the failure is described in the plural, “them,” as though the experts treated two separate puzzles instead of one message.

The scene foreshadows later confrontations. The magicians of Egypt would fail again before Moses, confessing “This is the finger of God” (Exodus 8:19), and the wise men of Babylon would admit that no man on earth could reveal the king’s matter (Daniel 2:10-11). Paul states the principle: “the things of God knoweth no man, but the Spirit of God” (1 Corinthians 2:11). Human learning has real value, but it cannot reach revelation that God has kept for himself. Pharaoh’s troubled spirit stands in contrast with the man in whom, he will soon confess, the Spirit of God dwells (v. 38).

wordNotes.term: וַתִּפָּעֶם רוּחוֹ (vattippa‘em rucho) — his spirit was troubled
wordNotes.explanation: Pa‘am means a beat, a step, or a time; in this passive form it describes inner agitation, a spirit that cannot settle. It is used again of Nebuchadnezzar after his dreams (Daniel 2:1, 3) and of the psalmist too troubled to speak (Psalm 77:4). Ruach, spirit, will reappear in verse 38, where Pharaoh recognises “the Spirit of God” in Joseph.

wordNotes.term: חַרְטֻמִּים (chartummim) — magicians
wordNotes.explanation: Borrowed from an Egyptian title for lector priests, the specialists who read sacred texts and spells and interpreted signs. The word occurs only of Egypt’s magicians in Genesis and Exodus (Exodus 7:11, 22; 8:18-19) and of the experts at Babylon’s court in Daniel (Daniel 1:20; 2:2). In each setting they cannot match what God reveals through his servant.

verses.bibleText: Then spake the chief butler unto Pharaoh, saying, I do remember my faults this day:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
With the court in confusion, the chief butler finally speaks: “I do remember my faults this day.” The Hebrew is more pointed: “My sins I am bringing to remembrance today.” The verb is the causative form of “remember,” the same form Joseph had used when he begged the butler to “make mention of me unto Pharaoh” (40:14). The request has waited two years for an answer, and the very words of Joseph’s plea come back in the butler’s mouth.

Which faults does he mean? Most obviously the offence that put him in prison in the first place (40:1), which he will now mention as tactfully as he can before the king he once offended. But the plural also covers his ingratitude. He had promised nothing in writing, yet Joseph had served him well and asked one kindness in return, and he had forgotten it. Recalling Joseph means admitting both. It is a risky speech for a courtier, because reminding Pharaoh of past displeasure could revive it.

The butler’s memory is not presented as a noble act. He speaks when it is useful to him and to Pharaoh, and he says nothing of Joseph’s innocence or of the God Joseph had confessed (40:8). Yet God uses even this belated and self-interested remembrance. The timing that seemed a cruel delay proves exact: had Joseph been released two years earlier, he might have been far away, or forgotten again, on the morning Pharaoh needed him. “He hath made every thing beautiful in his time” (Ecclesiastes 3:11). The human forgetting was real and wrong; the divine remembering was never in doubt.

wordNotes.term: אֶת־חֲטָאַי אֲנִי מַזְכִּיר (et-chata’ay ani mazkir) — I do remember my faults
wordNotes.explanation: Mazkir is the causative participle of zakhar, “to remember”: “I am causing to be remembered,” that is, “I must mention.” It echoes Joseph’s plea, vehizkartani, “make mention of me” (Genesis 40:14). Chata’ay, “my sins,” comes from the root used of the butler’s offence in 40:1. Later the title mazkir names the royal recorder, the official who brought matters to the king’s notice (2 Samuel 8:16).

verses.bibleText: Pharaoh was wroth with his servants, and put me in ward in the captain of the guard's house, both me and the chief baker:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The butler reminds Pharaoh of an incident the king had probably not forgotten: “Pharaoh was wroth with his servants, and put me in ward in the captain of the guard’s house, both me and the chief baker.” He uses the same verb for Pharaoh’s anger that the narrator used in 40:2, and the same location, the house of the captain of the guard. His account matches the story the reader already knows.

Notice the courtier’s caution. He speaks of himself in the third person as one of “his servants,” avoids saying what the offence was, and mentions the baker’s presence without naming his guilt. Before a king who held power of life and death, he takes no chances. He also omits any reference to Joseph as a fellow prisoner unjustly held. Those details would complicate his recommendation and perhaps raise uncomfortable questions about the justice of Potiphar’s household.

The verse places Joseph’s life within the conflicts of the court. The king’s anger, a cupbearer’s fall, a baker’s death, all seemingly unrelated to a Hebrew slave, were threads God was gathering. Proverbs warns that “the wrath of a king is as messengers of death” (Proverbs 16:14), and the baker had found that true. Yet the same royal anger that put two officials in Joseph’s prison became the means by which Joseph would reach the throne.

wordNotes.term: קָצַף (qatsaph) — was wroth
wordNotes.explanation: Qatsaph describes anger that boils over, often the anger of a superior against those under him. It is used of Pharaoh in Genesis 40:2, of Moses against disobedient Israelites (Exodus 16:20), and of God’s wrath against sin (Deuteronomy 9:19). The butler deliberately repeats the narrator’s word, recalling the king’s displeasure without describing its cause.

verses.bibleText: And we dreamed a dream in one night, I and he; we dreamed each man according to the interpretation of his dream.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And we dreamed a dream in one night, I and he.” The butler summarises chapter 40 in a single sentence. Two officials, one night, two dreams. The coincidence had seemed strange at the time, and the butler now sees that Pharaoh’s double dream stands in a similar situation. The court has gone from one unexplained pair of dreams to another.

“We dreamed each man according to the interpretation of his dream.” This phrase, repeated almost exactly from 40:5, means that each dream carried its own distinct meaning, fitted to the man who dreamed it. The butler’s dream was not a general sign but a personal message about his own future, and so was the baker’s. That point matters for his recommendation. If the young Hebrew could tell two men their separate fates from their separate dreams, he might be able to explain the king’s.

The butler’s words also contrast with what Joseph will say. The officials’ dreams had two different meanings; Pharaoh’s dreams have one (v. 25). The magicians had perhaps treated Pharaoh’s visions as two puzzles (v. 8). Joseph, guided by God, will see the unity.

wordNotes.term: אִישׁ כְּפִתְרוֹן חֲלֹמוֹ (’ish kefitron chalomo) — each man according to the interpretation of his dream
wordNotes.explanation: Pitron, interpretation, comes from patar, the verb for explaining a dream, and is found in the Old Testament only in the Joseph story (Genesis 40:5, 8; 41:11). The phrase means each dream carried its own meaning, suited to the dreamer. Aramaic and later Hebrew used a related word, pesher, for the interpretation of dreams and prophecies (Daniel 2:4).

verses.bibleText: And there was there with us a young man, an Hebrew, servant to the captain of the guard; and we told him, and he interpreted to us our dreams; to each man according to his dream he did interpret.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Now the butler introduces Joseph: “a young man, an Hebrew, servant to the captain of the guard.” Each description seems designed to lower expectations. A youth, a foreigner, a slave. The word “young man” could describe a servant of any age, but here it marks Joseph as junior and of no rank. “Hebrew” was the label Egyptians used of him with some contempt (39:14, 17), and the narrator later notes that Egyptians would not eat with Hebrews (43:32). “Servant to the captain of the guard” describes his legal status without mentioning that he was a prisoner.

Yet the speech carries an unintended tribute. This despised young foreigner did what Egypt’s experts could not: “we told him, and he interpreted to us our dreams.” The butler repeats the point, “to each man according to his dream he did interpret,” stressing the precision of Joseph’s readings. He does not say, as Joseph had insisted, that “interpretations belong to God” (40:8). In his telling Joseph appears simply as a gifted interpreter.

Scripture often shows God choosing what the world overlooks. Paul writes that “God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise” and “base things of the world, and things which are despised” (1 Corinthians 1:27-28). David was the youngest son left with the sheep; Daniel was a captive youth in Babylon. The Hebrew slave in the prison was God’s chosen instrument for the most powerful court on earth.

wordNotes.term: נַעַר עִבְרִי (na‘ar ‘ivri) — a young man, an Hebrew
wordNotes.explanation: Na‘ar can mean a boy, a young man, or a servant; Joseph was called a na‘ar at seventeen (Genesis 37:2), and the word could be used dismissively. ‘Ivri, Hebrew, first described Abram (Genesis 14:13) and is used mainly when foreigners speak of Israelites or when Israelites identify themselves to outsiders (Genesis 39:14; Jonah 1:9).

verses.bibleText: And it came to pass, as he interpreted to us, so it was; me he restored unto mine office, and him he hanged.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The butler’s testimony ends with the decisive proof: “as he interpreted to us, so it was.” Joseph’s word had come true exactly. The butler was restored to his post, and the baker was hanged. The test of a prophet in Israel would later be stated in just these terms: if the word comes to pass, it is from the Lord (Deuteronomy 18:22; Jeremiah 28:9). Here a pagan official unknowingly applies that test and finds Joseph’s interpretations reliable.

The Hebrew wording, “me he restored unto mine office, and him he hanged,” is ambiguous about who did the restoring and hanging. Pharaoh carried out the sentences, but the phrasing allows the sense that Joseph’s word, as an accurate prediction, determined them. The ancient world often credited a prophet with what his word announced, as when Jeremiah was told he had been set “to root out, and to pull down” by speaking (Jeremiah 1:10).

The butler’s experience becomes evidence that prepares Pharaoh to trust Joseph. Two years earlier his fate and his companion’s had been opposite, and Joseph had told each the truth without flattery. For the baker the truth was terrible. A man who would deliver bad news honestly to a condemned official is a man a king could trust to tell him the truth about Egypt’s future, whether good or bad.

wordNotes.term: כַּאֲשֶׁר פָּתַר־לָנוּ כֵּן הָיָה (ka’asher patar-lanu ken hayah) — as he interpreted to us, so it was
wordNotes.explanation: A compact formula of fulfilment: “just as he interpreted, so it happened.” The pairing ka’asher … ken, “as … so,” is used throughout Scripture to show that events matched a word spoken beforehand (Genesis 1:7, 9 use a related “and it was so”). Joseph’s words had the reliability that Scripture later requires of true prophecy (Deuteronomy 18:22; 1 Samuel 3:19).

verses.bibleText: Then Pharaoh sent and called Joseph, and they brought him hastily out of the dungeon: and he shaved himself, and changed his raiment, and came in unto Pharaoh.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The pace suddenly quickens: “Then Pharaoh sent and called Joseph, and they brought him hastily out of the dungeon.” The verb literally means “they made him run.” After thirteen years of slow suffering, deliverance arrives in a rush. The word translated “dungeon” is bor, the pit, the same word used for the empty cistern into which his brothers threw him (37:24) and for his own description of the prison in his plea to the butler (40:15). Joseph is drawn up from the pit for a second time, now to stand before a king.

Before he appears, “he shaved himself, and changed his raiment.” Egyptians were clean-shaven, and Egyptian art shows Asiatic foreigners with beards and long hair. To appear before Pharaoh, Joseph must be made presentable by Egyptian standards. The change of clothing is significant in a story where garments mark every turn: the coat of many colours stripped from him (37:23), the garment left in the hand of Potiphar’s wife (39:12), and soon the fine linen of a ruler (v. 42). His old clothes belonged to slavery and prison; the new ones belong to the court.

The movement of this verse, from the pit to the presence of the king, forms the hinge of Joseph’s life. The Scriptures repeatedly trace this pattern of humiliation followed by exaltation, and it finds its fullest expression in Christ. He “humbled himself, and became obedient unto death,” and was laid in the grave; “wherefore God also hath highly exalted him” (Philippians 2:8-9). Joseph’s rescue does not stand as a detailed allegory of Christ’s resurrection, but its shape, an innocent sufferer brought up from the place of death to the right hand of the throne, prepares the reader to understand the greater story. Peter states the principle for all God’s people: “Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time” (1 Peter 5:6).

wordNotes.term: וַיְרִיצֻהוּ מִן־הַבּוֹר (vayritsuhu min-habbor) — they brought him hastily out of the dungeon
wordNotes.explanation: Vayritsuhu is the causative of ruts, “to run”: “they made him run.” Bor means a pit or cistern, used of the dry pit at Dothan (Genesis 37:24) and of Joseph’s prison (40:15). It also becomes an image for the grave and deep distress, from which the psalmist praises God for lifting him (Psalm 40:2; Psalm 30:3).

verses.bibleText: And Pharaoh said unto Joseph, I have dreamed a dream, and there is none that can interpret it: and I have heard say of thee, that thou canst understand a dream to interpret it.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Pharaoh comes straight to the point: “I have dreamed a dream, and there is none that can interpret it: and I have heard say of thee, that thou canst understand a dream to interpret it.” The most powerful man in the world confesses his helplessness to a prisoner who arrived minutes earlier. He speaks of “a dream,” singular, already sensing that his two visions belong together.

The second half of his statement is a compliment, and a dangerous one. Literally Pharaoh says, “you hear a dream to interpret it,” that is, as soon as you hear a dream you can explain it. The butler’s report has made Joseph into a master interpreter with an infallible skill. Here is an opportunity for Joseph to secure his future by accepting the reputation. Any prisoner hoping for release would be tempted to claim as much ability as the king believed he had.

The absence of an interpreter in the conversation may suggest that Joseph by now spoke Egyptian fluently, after more than a decade in an Egyptian household and prison. Later he will deliberately use an interpreter with his brothers to hide his identity (42:23). Joseph’s years of hidden suffering had also been years of preparation. Moses would later be “learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians” before God used him (Acts 7:22), and Joseph, too, had been schooled in the language and customs of the land he would govern.

wordNotes.term: תִּשְׁמַע חֲלוֹם לִפְתֹּר אֹתוֹ (tishma‘ chalom liftor ’oto) — thou canst understand a dream to interpret it
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “you hear a dream to interpret it.” Shama‘, to hear, often carries the sense of understanding (Genesis 11:7; 42:23). Pharaoh credits Joseph with the ability to grasp any dream the moment it is told. Belshazzar later says something similar to Daniel, “I have heard of thee, that thou canst make interpretations” (Daniel 5:16), and Daniel, like Joseph, points beyond himself.

verses.bibleText: And Joseph answered Pharaoh, saying, It is not in me: God shall give Pharaoh an answer of peace.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Joseph’s first words before the throne are among the most important in his life: “It is not in me: God shall give Pharaoh an answer of peace.” In Hebrew the opening is a single word, bil‘aday, “apart from me” or “not I.” Before Pharaoh has even described the dream, Joseph refuses the reputation the king has offered him. He has no secret technique, no special skill he can claim as his own. He does have confidence, but it is confidence in God.

This is the same conviction he expressed in the prison: “Do not interpretations belong to God?” (40:8). Two years of disappointment had not soured it. Now, standing before a man who believed himself divine and who was surrounded by priests of many gods, Joseph names one God as the source of the answer. He is humble and fearless at once. To say “not I” before a king who could free or execute him took more courage than to promise an interpretation. Daniel would later stand in the same place before Nebuchadnezzar: “there is a God in heaven that revealeth secrets,” and “this secret is not revealed to me for any wisdom that I have” (Daniel 2:28, 30).

“An answer of peace” is literally “the peace (shalom) of Pharaoh.” Joseph assures the king that God will answer concerning his welfare, or will give an answer that sets his troubled spirit at rest. Even before hearing the dream, Joseph is sure that God intends good by it. The dream will announce famine, but it is a warning given in time to prepare, and so an act of mercy toward Egypt. Some ancient translations read Joseph’s words as “Without God, Pharaoh will not be answered with peace,” which makes the same point from another angle.

Paul states the principle that governed Joseph: “Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think any thing as of ourselves; but our sufficiency is of God” (2 Corinthians 3:5). Every gift God gives is meant to direct attention back to the Giver. Jesus himself said, “I can of mine own self do nothing” (John 5:30), and sought the glory of the Father who sent him. The servant who refuses glory for himself is the servant God can safely exalt.

wordNotes.term: בִּלְעָדָי (bil‘aday) — it is not in me
wordNotes.explanation: A compound meaning “apart from me” or “not I,” used here as a one-word exclamation. Abraham uses the same form when he refuses the king of Sodom’s goods: “Save only that which the young men have eaten” (Genesis 14:24, bil‘aday). Joseph refuses credit as Abraham refused reward. The Septuagint renders the thought with “Without God,” stressing that the answer depends wholly on him.

wordNotes.term: אֶת־שְׁלוֹם פַּרְעֹה (’et-shelom par‘oh) — an answer of peace
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “God will answer the peace of Pharaoh.” Shalom means wholeness and well-being, not merely the absence of conflict. Joseph had once been sent to ask after his brothers’ shalom (Genesis 37:14), though they could not speak shalom to him (37:4). Now he promises that God’s answer will concern Pharaoh’s welfare and bring his troubled spirit rest (compare Jeremiah 29:11).

verses.bibleText: And Pharaoh said unto Joseph, In my dream, behold, I stood upon the bank of the river:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Pharaoh now tells Joseph what the reader has already heard in verses 1-7. Genesis often repeats a scene through a character’s eyes, and the differences reveal the speaker’s state of mind. The retelling also slows the story at the moment of greatest suspense, so that the reader waits with Pharaoh for the answer.

The first change is small but telling. The narrator had said Pharaoh stood “by the river” (v. 1); Pharaoh says, “I stood upon the bank of the river,” literally “on the lip of the Nile.” The detail places him at the very edge of the water, the boundary between the river that gives life and the land that receives it. He speaks of “my dream,” singular, already convinced that the two visions form one message. He has accepted Joseph’s promise that God will answer, and he tells the dream to the one person in Egypt who has pointed him beyond Egypt’s gods.

wordNotes.term: עַל־שְׂפַת הַיְאֹר (‘al-sefat hay’or) — upon the bank of the river
wordNotes.explanation: Safah means a lip, and by extension the edge or shore of water. The same word describes “the sand which is upon the sea shore” in God’s promise to Abraham (Genesis 22:17) and the bank of the Nile where Moses was found (Exodus 2:3). Pharaoh’s wording is more vivid than the narrator’s, as befits an eyewitness.

verses.bibleText: And, behold, there came up out of the river seven kine, fatfleshed and well favoured; and they fed in a meadow:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Pharaoh’s description of the first seven cows follows the narrator’s account almost word for word: they came up out of the river, “fatfleshed and well favoured,” and fed in the reed grass. The only change is the order of the two adjectives, which are reversed from verse 2. The good half of the dream needed no embellishment. It was the picture of a normal, prosperous year in Egypt, the kind of scene every Pharaoh hoped would describe his reign.

Egyptian kings liked to claim that no one went hungry in their years because the gods favoured them. A herd of fat cows coming out of a full river was a royal boast in picture form. Pharaoh lingers only briefly on it, for it is not the part that troubles him. The weight of his speech falls on what follows.

wordNotes.term: בְּרִיאוֹת בָּשָׂר וִיפֹת תֹּאַר (beri’ot basar vifot to’ar) — fatfleshed and well favoured
wordNotes.explanation: Pharaoh reverses the order of verse 2 and uses to’ar, form, for “favour,” instead of mar’eh, appearance. Both are used together of Joseph’s own good looks: he was “a goodly person, and well favoured” (Genesis 39:6). The variation in wording shows careful storytelling, retelling the scene without mere copying (compare 1 Samuel 16:18).

verses.bibleText: And, behold, seven other kine came up after them, poor and very ill favoured and leanfleshed, such as I never saw in all the land of Egypt for badness:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Here Pharaoh’s retelling expands. The narrator had called the second herd “ill favoured and leanfleshed” (v. 3). Pharaoh piles up words: “poor and very ill favoured and leanfleshed, such as I never saw in all the land of Egypt for badness.” He adds “poor,” a word used of the weak and needy, and intensifies “ill favoured” with “very.” Then he breaks into a personal exclamation of disgust.

The addition reveals how badly the dream has shaken him. A king who had surveyed all the herds of Egypt had never seen anything like these animals. They are not merely thin; they are a kind of ugliness outside his experience. Without knowing it, Pharaoh is describing a famine worse than anything Egypt remembers, which is exactly what Joseph will announce: “it shall be very grievous” (v. 31). The god-king of Egypt stands before his own nightmare, frightened and unable to explain it.

wordNotes.term: דַּלּוֹת (dallot) — poor
wordNotes.explanation: Dal describes what is weak, low, or impoverished. It is often used of poor people whom God defends and commands his people to protect (Exodus 23:3; Psalm 41:1). Of cattle it means scrawny and feeble. Pharaoh’s choice of a word associated with poverty fits the meaning Joseph will give: years when the land itself is reduced to want.

verses.bibleText: And the lean and the ill favoured kine did eat up the first seven fat kine:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Pharaoh repeats the shocking climax of the first dream: “the lean and the ill favoured kine did eat up the first seven fat kine.” He adds the word “first,” pointing to the order of events. The good came first and the bad came after. That sequence is essential to the meaning. If famine came first, it would simply be a hard season followed by recovery. Because plenty comes first, there is a window in which to prepare, and that window will become the subject of Joseph’s counsel (vv. 33-36).

The line is brief, and Pharaoh seems to hurry past it toward the detail that disturbed him most, which he will describe in the next verse.

wordNotes.term: הָרִאשֹׁנוֹת (hari’shonot) — the first
wordNotes.explanation: Ri’shon means first in order or time. Pharaoh’s addition highlights the sequence: seven good years come first, then seven bad. The same word marks the “first” things God brings to pass before announcing new ones (Isaiah 42:9), and here it underlines that the years of plenty are the time given to prepare (Genesis 41:29-30).

verses.bibleText: And when they had eaten them up, it could not be known that they had eaten them; but they were still ill favoured, as at the beginning. So I awoke.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
This whole verse is new. The narrator had said nothing about what happened after the lean cows ate the fat ones. Pharaoh adds: “when they had eaten them up, it could not be known that they had eaten them; but they were still ill favoured, as at the beginning.” The lean cows gained nothing. They swallowed seven fat animals and looked as starved as before.

This is the most unsettling image in the dream, and it carries the heart of the interpretation. Joseph will explain that “all the plenty shall be forgotten” and “shall not be known in the land by reason of that famine” (vv. 30-31). The abundance of seven good years will be consumed so completely that no one will be able to tell it ever existed. The narrator held this detail back so that the reader hears it at the moment it matters most, just before Joseph answers. “So I awoke,” Pharaoh says, recalling the shock that ended the first dream.

wordNotes.term: וְלֹא נוֹדַע כִּי־בָאוּ אֶל־קִרְבֶּנָה (velo’ noda‘ ki-va’u ’el-qirbenah) — it could not be known that they had eaten them
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “it was not known that they had gone into their inward parts.” Yada‘, to know, in its passive form means “to be perceived.” Joseph repeats the idea when he says the plenty “shall not be known” (Genesis 41:31). Haggai describes the same futility in Israel’s later famine: “ye eat, but ye have not enough” (Haggai 1:6).

verses.bibleText: And I saw in my dream, and, behold, seven ears came up in one stalk, full and good:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Pharaoh turns to the second dream with a simple “And I saw in my dream.” He does not say, as the narrator did, that he slept and dreamed a second time (v. 5). For him there is one dream with two scenes. That instinct is correct, and Joseph will confirm it: “the dream is one” (v. 26).

The ears of grain are described as “full and good,” a slightly different pair of words from the narrator’s “rank and good.” “Full” anticipates the meaning: the heads are filled with grain, the very harvest that Joseph will gather into the cities. Seven heads on one stalk again picture an abundance beyond the ordinary.

wordNotes.term: מְלֵאֹת וְטֹבוֹת (mele’ot vetovot) — full and good
wordNotes.explanation: Male’, full, describes something filled to capacity. The narrator used the same word together with “rank” in verse 7 for the ears that were swallowed. Here it replaces “rank,” emphasising heads packed with grain. The image matches the harvest of the plentiful years, when the earth brought forth “by handfuls” (Genesis 41:47; compare Psalm 65:9).

verses.bibleText: And, behold, seven ears, withered, thin, and blasted with the east wind, sprung up after them:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Again Pharaoh intensifies the bad half of the dream. The narrator had called the second ears “thin and blasted with the east wind” (v. 6). Pharaoh says they were “withered, thin, and blasted with the east wind.” The added word “withered” means hard and shrivelled, ears with no life in them. Three terms now describe the blighted grain, as three described the poor cows in verse 19.

The pattern is consistent. Pharaoh reports the good parts of the dream plainly and the bad parts with growing alarm. His retelling is not a neutral record but the speech of a man frightened by what he has seen. That fear is itself part of God’s purpose: a warning that did not trouble its hearer would not move him to act.

wordNotes.term: צְנֻמוֹת (tsenumot) — withered
wordNotes.explanation: This word occurs only here in the Old Testament. Related forms in other Semitic languages mean hard or dried out, so it probably describes ears shrunken and hardened by heat. It is Pharaoh’s own addition to the narrator’s description (Genesis 41:6), and it intensifies the picture of blight in the manner of the psalmist’s “withered like grass” (Psalm 102:4).

verses.bibleText: And the thin ears devoured the seven good ears: and I told this unto the magicians; but there was none that could declare it to me.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Pharaoh closes his account where he began it: “the thin ears devoured the seven good ears: and I told this unto the magicians; but there was none that could declare it to me.” The confession of verse 15 frames the whole retelling. Egypt’s experts had heard everything Joseph has now heard, and they had nothing to say.

The verb changes from “interpret” to “declare,” a word meaning to make known or to tell plainly. Joseph will use the same verb in his reply: “God hath shewed Pharaoh what he is about to do” (v. 25). The magicians could not declare; God has already declared. The retelling thus ends by setting the failure of human wisdom beside the revelation that is about to be given, the same contrast Isaiah draws between idols that cannot announce the future and the Lord who declares the end from the beginning (Isaiah 41:22-23; 46:10).

wordNotes.term: וְאֵין מַגִּיד לִי (ve’en maggid li) — none that could declare it to me
wordNotes.explanation: Maggid is the participle of nagad, “to tell, make known.” The magicians had no declaration; in the next verse Joseph says God has “shewed” (higgid, the same verb) Pharaoh his purpose. Isaiah uses this verb when he challenges idols to “shew us what shall happen” and proclaims that the Lord alone declares the future (Isaiah 41:22; 46:10).

verses.bibleText: And Joseph said unto Pharaoh, The dream of Pharaoh is one: God hath shewed Pharaoh what he is about to do.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Joseph answers without hesitation. He asks no questions, consults no manuals, and takes no time to deliberate. His first statement establishes the key: “The dream of Pharaoh is one.” The cows and the ears are not two messages but a single message given twice. The magicians may have puzzled over two dreams; Joseph sees one.

His second statement names the source and the purpose: “God hath shewed Pharaoh what he is about to do.” This is the most important sentence in the interpretation, and Joseph will repeat it in verse 28 and reinforce it in verse 32. The dream is not an omen from the Nile, a message from the grain gods, or a product of the king’s anxious mind. It is a revelation from the one God, and its content is God’s own coming action. The famine will not be an accident of nature but a work of the Lord who governs the seasons. Joseph speaks of “God” (Elohim), the general name that a foreign king could understand, but he leaves no doubt that this God stands above every power in Egypt.

The idea that God reveals his purposes beforehand runs through Scripture. “Shall I hide from Abraham that thing which I do?” the Lord asked before Sodom’s destruction (18:17). “he revealeth his secret unto his servants the prophets” (Amos 3:7). In this case God reveals his plan to a pagan king through his servant, and he does so for the sake of saving life. The God of Abraham cares for Egypt too, and the warning is an act of grace to a nation that did not know him.

wordNotes.term: חֲלוֹם פַּרְעֹה אֶחָד הוּא (chalom par‘oh ’echad hu’) — the dream of Pharaoh is one
wordNotes.explanation: ’Echad, one, is the word used of the unity of God himself (Deuteronomy 6:4) and of the man and woman becoming “one flesh” (Genesis 2:24). Here it declares that both dreams share a single meaning. Joseph repeats the point at the end of verse 26, framing his explanation of the details with the statement of their unity (compare Genesis 41:32).

wordNotes.term: הִגִּיד לְפַרְעֹה (higgid lefar‘oh) — hath shewed Pharaoh
wordNotes.explanation: Higgid comes from nagad, “to make known, declare.” It answers Pharaoh’s complaint that no one could “declare” the dream to him (Genesis 41:24). The magicians had nothing to tell; God had already told. The same verb names the task Nebuchadnezzar later demanded of his own experts, “to shew the king his dreams” (Daniel 2:2), and Isaiah’s challenge to the idols to “shew the things that are to come” (Isaiah 41:23).

verses.bibleText: The seven good kine are seven years; and the seven good ears are seven years: the dream is one.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Now Joseph explains the symbols. “The seven good kine are seven years; and the seven good ears are seven years.” The interpretation is simple once it is given. Each animal and each ear stands for a year, and the good ones stand for good years. Joseph does not explain how he knows this. The certainty comes from the God who gave the dream, as he had already told Pharaoh (v. 16).

He ends the verse as he ended the previous one: “the dream is one.” The repetition frames the explanation. Whatever details follow, the reader must keep the unity in view. Two pictures, one prophecy.

Scripture sometimes uses days or animals or objects as symbols for periods of time, and the meaning is always given by revelation, not by guesswork. Daniel’s visions of beasts and horns, for example, are interpreted by a heavenly messenger (Daniel 7:16-17; 8:20-21). The principle is the same here: the symbols mean what God says they mean. Joseph’s plain explanation is a model of sober interpretation. He does not elaborate the meaning of cows and ears beyond what the dream requires.

wordNotes.term: שֶׁבַע שָׁנִים הֵנָּה (sheva‘ shanim hennah) — are seven years
wordNotes.explanation: The Hebrew links symbol and meaning with a simple pronoun: “seven years they are.” The same direct formula appears when Joseph explained the cupbearer’s branches and the baker’s baskets as three days (Genesis 40:12, 18) and when Daniel explains a vision’s parts (Daniel 2:38). Seven, a number of completeness since creation’s week (Genesis 2:2), marks two full periods.

verses.bibleText: And the seven thin and ill favoured kine that came up after them are seven years; and the seven empty ears blasted with the east wind shall be seven years of famine.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The second half of the interpretation: “the seven thin and ill favoured kine that came up after them are seven years; and the seven empty ears blasted with the east wind shall be seven years of famine.” Joseph now uses the word the whole dream has been building toward: famine. He also describes the ears as “empty,” a fresh word that captures their meaning better than any picture: there is nothing in them.

Famine was a recurring threat in the ancient world, and Genesis has already recorded famines that drove Abraham and Isaac from Canaan (12:10; 26:1). Egypt was usually the refuge in such times because its river kept flowing when the rains failed in Canaan. This famine will be different. It will strike Egypt itself, and the narrator will later note that it reached “all lands” (v. 54). Records from Egypt mention long periods of low floods and hunger, and one later inscription even recalls a seven-year famine in an earlier age. Joseph’s word places the coming disaster within God’s purpose rather than leaving it as blind fate.

wordNotes.term: הָרֵקוֹת (hareqot) — empty
wordNotes.explanation: Req means empty or worthless. It describes the dry pit into which Joseph was thrown: “the pit was empty, there was no water in it” (Genesis 37:24), and empty vessels (2 Kings 4:3). Here it replaces “thin” and states the meaning plainly: ears with no grain. God promised Israel that his word would never return to him “void,” using a related word (Isaiah 55:11).

wordNotes.term: רָעָב (ra‘av) — famine
wordNotes.explanation: Ra‘av means hunger and famine, the condition of a land without food. The word occurs repeatedly in Genesis 41–47, dominating the rest of the Joseph story. Earlier famines drove Abraham and Isaac toward Egypt (Genesis 12:10; 26:1). Later prophets speak of famine as one of God’s judgements, and Amos warns of a worse famine “of hearing the words of the LORD” (Amos 8:11).

verses.bibleText: This is the thing which I have spoken unto Pharaoh: What God is about to do he sheweth unto Pharaoh.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“This is the thing which I have spoken unto Pharaoh: What God is about to do he sheweth unto Pharaoh.” Joseph repeats his central statement from verse 25 almost exactly, with one change in the verb. In verse 25 God “hath shewed,” that is, declared; here God “sheweth,” literally “causes to see.” The first word stresses that God has told Pharaoh his purpose; the second stresses that God has let him see it in vision. Together they say that the dream was revelation in both word and picture.

The repetition is purposeful. Joseph will not let Pharaoh forget the source of the dream, even as he moves into the details of the coming years. His interpretation begins with God (v. 25), returns to God here at its midpoint, and ends with God twice in verse 32. A king who considered himself a god is told three times that another God controls his future.

The principle that God alone can announce what he will do is central to Scripture’s distinction between the true God and idols. “I am God, and there is none like me, declaring the end from the beginning” (Isaiah 46:9-10). A god who cannot control the future cannot announce it with certainty. Joseph’s confidence rests not on his own insight but on the character of the God he serves.

wordNotes.term: הֶרְאָה אֶת־פַּרְעֹה (her’ah ’et-par‘oh) — he sheweth unto Pharaoh
wordNotes.explanation: Her’ah is the causative of ra’ah, “to see”: God “caused Pharaoh to see.” It differs from higgid in verse 25, which stresses making known by word. The causative of ra’ah is used of God showing Abram the land and Moses the pattern of the tabernacle (Genesis 12:1; Exodus 25:9), and of visions given to prophets (Amos 7:1).

verses.bibleText: Behold, there come seven years of great plenty throughout all the land of Egypt:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Joseph now spells out what the dream foretells, beginning with good news: “Behold, there come seven years of great plenty throughout all the land of Egypt.” He uses the word “behold” that ran through the dream itself, as if to say, “Look, this is what you saw.” The years of plenty will not be patchy or regional; they will cover “all the land of Egypt.”

This is the promised “answer of peace” (v. 16). For seven years Pharaoh will enjoy the prosperity every king desired. Yet Joseph gives the good years a single verse, while the famine will receive three (vv. 30-32). The proportion matches Pharaoh’s own retelling, which lingered on the lean cows and the withered ears. Plenty is a gift, but it is not the point of the message. It is the opportunity God provides before the trial arrives. Scripture repeatedly links abundance with responsibility: the God who gives wealth also tests what his people do with it (Deuteronomy 8:10-18; Luke 12:16-21).

Joseph’s counsel will treat these years as a trust rather than a windfall. Everything Egypt harvests in them comes from God, and the right use of it is to set aside part for the time when the fields fail. David confessed the same truth when Israel gave freely for the temple: “all things come of thee, and of thine own have we given thee” (1 Chronicles 29:14). The believer who prospers is a steward, not an owner, called to use what God supplies for the good of others (1 Peter 4:10).

wordNotes.term: שָׂבָע גָּדוֹל (sava‘ gadol) — great plenty
wordNotes.explanation: Sava‘ means fullness or satisfaction, the condition of having eaten enough. The verb from the same root describes Israel eating and being full in the land God gives (Deuteronomy 8:10), and Proverbs promises barns filled with plenty to those who honour God with their substance (Proverbs 3:10). In Genesis 41 the word is used of the seven good years (vv. 29-31, 34, 47, 53).

verses.bibleText: And there shall arise after them seven years of famine; and all the plenty shall be forgotten in the land of Egypt; and the famine shall consume the land;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Then the warning: “there shall arise after them seven years of famine; and all the plenty shall be forgotten in the land of Egypt; and the famine shall consume the land.” The verb “arise” is the same word used for the lean cows rising out of the river. The famine is pictured as something that comes up and stands over the land.

The most striking phrase is “all the plenty shall be forgotten.” This is the meaning of the strange detail in Pharaoh’s retelling, that the lean cows looked as starved as ever after eating the fat ones (v. 21). The famine will be so severe that people will not even remember that there were good years. Memory itself will be swallowed up. Then Joseph says, “the famine shall consume the land,” using a word that means to finish off or bring to an end. The image is total exhaustion.

Forgetting is a recurring theme in this part of the story. The butler forgot Joseph (40:23); Egypt will forget its plenty; Joseph will name his son “Forgetting” (v. 51). In each case forgetting shows how fragile human memory and gratitude are. The good years would be lost entirely unless someone remembered them in advance and set aside their fruit.

wordNotes.term: וְנִשְׁכַּח כָּל־הַשָּׂבָע (venishkach kol-hassava‘) — all the plenty shall be forgotten
wordNotes.explanation: Shakhach, to forget, links this verse to the butler who “forgat” Joseph (Genesis 40:23) and to Manasseh, whose name praises God for making Joseph forget his toil (41:51). Moses would later warn Israel that full stomachs lead to forgetting the Lord who gave the plenty (Deuteronomy 8:11-14).

wordNotes.term: וְכִלָּה הָרָעָב (vekhillah hara‘av) — the famine shall consume
wordNotes.explanation: Kalah, in this intensive form, means to bring to an end, use up, or destroy completely. The same verb describes God finishing his work of creation (Genesis 2:2) and the water running out of Hagar’s skin (Genesis 21:15). Here it pictures famine exhausting the land until nothing remains.

verses.bibleText: And the plenty shall not be known in the land by reason of that famine following; for it shall be very grievous.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Joseph restates the point in fresh words to drive it home: “the plenty shall not be known in the land by reason of that famine following; for it shall be very grievous.” The phrase “shall not be known” matches Pharaoh’s own words about the lean cows: “it could not be known that they had eaten them” (v. 21). Joseph shows that he has listened carefully to every detail of the dream and found its meaning.

“Very grievous” translates a word meaning “heavy.” The famine will weigh on the land like a burden too great to bear. The same word described the famine in Abraham’s day (12:10) and will describe this famine again in the chapters that follow (43:1; 47:4, 13). Joseph does not soften the prospect. He tells the king plainly how bad things will become. Honest warning, even when unwelcome, is a mark of a faithful messenger. The false prophets of Jeremiah’s time cried “Peace, peace” when there was no peace (Jeremiah 6:14). Joseph’s “answer of peace” is real precisely because it includes the hard truth.

wordNotes.term: כָבֵד הוּא מְאֹד (khaved hu’ me’od) — it shall be very grievous
wordNotes.explanation: Kaved means heavy, weighty, or severe. It describes famine in Genesis 12:10 and 43:1, and the “grievous” plagues on Egypt (Exodus 9:3). The same root gives the word for glory, the weight of honour (Genesis 45:13). The famine’s heaviness will be matched by the weight of honour Joseph receives as its manager.

verses.bibleText: And for that the dream was doubled unto Pharaoh twice; it is because the thing is established by God, and God will shortly bring it to pass.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Joseph now explains why the dream came twice: “for that the dream was doubled unto Pharaoh twice; it is because the thing is established by God, and God will shortly bring it to pass.” Repetition means certainty and urgency. The thing is “established,” fixed and settled, beyond any possibility of change. And God will act “shortly,” hastening to bring it about.

This sentence explains every pair of dreams in Joseph’s story, including his own. His dreams of sheaves and stars had also been doubled (37:5-9). Joseph had now waited thirteen years without seeing those dreams fulfilled. Yet here he declares with full confidence that a doubled dream is a settled matter with God. The reader cannot help noticing what this implies about Joseph’s own future. The God who fixes Egypt’s harvests has also fixed the day when Joseph’s brothers will bow before him (42:6).

The verse also holds together divine sovereignty and human responsibility. God has determined the famine; it will come whatever Pharaoh does. Yet that certainty is not a reason for passivity. It is the very reason Joseph immediately urges action (v. 33). Because the future is in God’s hands and he has revealed it, wise people prepare. Faith in God’s control does not make planning unnecessary; it makes planning meaningful. Jesus gave signs of the end so that his followers might watch and be ready (Matthew 24:32-33, 44).

Joseph names God twice in this one verse. His interpretation has begun with God, returned to God, and now ends with God. The king of Egypt has been told, in the plainest terms, who rules the Nile.

What holds for Pharaoh’s dream holds for the whole prophetic word. When God declares the future, his people may build on it with confidence. Peter calls the prophetic Scriptures “a more sure word of prophecy,” a light shining in a dark place until the day dawns (2 Peter 1:19). The certainty of what God has spoken, including the promise of Christ’s return, is meant to awaken watchfulness and faithful work, never idle waiting.

wordNotes.term: נָכוֹן הַדָּבָר מֵעִם הָאֱלֹהִים (nakhon haddavar me‘im ha’elohim) — the thing is established by God
wordNotes.explanation: Nakhon is a passive participle of kun, to be firm or fixed. It describes what is settled and certain, like the dawn that is “prepared as the morning” (Hosea 6:3) or a throne “established” for ever (Psalm 93:2). Me‘im, “from with,” places the decision in God’s own presence. Nothing on earth can overturn what has been fixed there.

wordNotes.term: וּמְמַהֵר הָאֱלֹהִים (umemaher ha’elohim) — God will shortly bring it to pass
wordNotes.explanation: Memaher is a participle of mahar, to hasten: “God is hastening to do it.” The same verb describes Abraham hurrying to welcome his guests (Genesis 18:6). God’s timing is never careless; when his appointed hour arrives, he acts without delay (Habakkuk 2:3; Isaiah 60:22).

verses.bibleText: Now therefore let Pharaoh look out a man discreet and wise, and set him over the land of Egypt.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Joseph has answered the question Pharaoh asked. Now he goes further and offers counsel nobody requested: “Now therefore let Pharaoh look out a man discreet and wise, and set him over the land of Egypt.” The words “now therefore” mark the shift from revelation to response. Because God has fixed the future, Pharaoh must act.

The advice was bold. A prisoner summoned to explain a dream had no standing to tell the king how to govern. Joseph nonetheless speaks with the same directness he showed in refusing credit for the interpretation. He frames everything carefully around Pharaoh’s authority, “let Pharaoh” look out a man, “let Pharaoh” do this (v. 34), and he does not put himself forward. His concern is that the warning God has given should not be wasted.

The qualities he names matter. The man must be “discreet,” literally discerning, able to see how causes lead to effects, and “wise,” skilled in carrying out what he understands. Pharaoh had just found that his own wise men could not even explain the dream. Joseph’s counsel implies that knowledge of the future is useless without someone who can turn it into a plan. Later the same pair of words describes the gift God gave Solomon for governing his people (1 Kings 3:12), and Moses asks Israel’s tribes for men who are “wise and understanding” to lead them (Deuteronomy 1:13). True wisdom in Scripture is practical. It begins with the fear of the Lord (Proverbs 9:10) and shows itself in faithful decisions.

wordNotes.term: אִישׁ נָבוֹן וְחָכָם (’ish navon vechakham) — a man discreet and wise
wordNotes.explanation: Navon, from bin, to discern, describes a person who perceives and distinguishes; chakham, wise, describes skill in applying knowledge. The pair recurs in Pharaoh’s reply (Genesis 41:39), in Moses’ call for leaders (Deuteronomy 1:13), and in reverse order in God’s gift to Solomon of “a wise and an understanding heart” (1 Kings 3:12). Wisdom in this sense is the ability to rule well under God.

verses.bibleText: Let Pharaoh do this, and let him appoint officers over the land, and take up the fifth part of the land of Egypt in the seven plenteous years.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Joseph outlines the plan in practical steps. First, Pharaoh should “appoint officers over the land,” overseers in each region who would answer to the chief administrator. Second, they should “take up the fifth part of the land of Egypt in the seven plenteous years.” A fifth, twenty per cent, of every harvest would be set aside during the good years.

The proportion was well judged. In years of exceptional abundance, a fifth could be taken without hardship to the farmers, while seven years of such collection would build a vast reserve. A heavier levy might have provoked resistance; a lighter one would not have lasted seven lean years. Egypt already had a long tradition of taxing harvests according to the height of the Nile flood, so Joseph’s plan built on existing practice rather than inventing a new system. The same fraction later appears as a permanent arrangement in Egypt (47:24, 26).

The verse is a model of foresight. Joseph does not wait for the famine to begin before thinking about food. He acts while there is still plenty to spare. Proverbs praises the ant that “provideth her meat in the summer, and gathereth her food in the harvest” (Proverbs 6:8), and warns that “a prudent man foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself” (Proverbs 22:3). The years of plenty were themselves God’s gift, and so was the warning that came with them. Faithful stewardship receives both, saving from the abundance for the need that is sure to come.

wordNotes.term: וְחִמֵּשׁ אֶת־אֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם (vechimmesh ’et-’erets mitsrayim) — take up the fifth part of the land of Egypt
wordNotes.explanation: Chimmesh is a verb formed from chamesh, five, and means “to take a fifth.” It occurs only here. The noun for “fifth” reappears when the arrangement becomes Egypt’s permanent law (Genesis 47:24, 26). In Israel a fifth was added when restoring something wrongly taken (Leviticus 5:16), but the context here is simply prudent taxation of an abundant harvest.

wordNotes.term: פְּקִדִים (peqidim) — officers
wordNotes.explanation: From paqad, to visit, appoint, or oversee. A paqid is someone given charge over others or over a task. The same root describes Joseph being made overseer in Potiphar’s house (Genesis 39:4-5) and the officers Ahasuerus appointed to gather young women (Esther 2:3). Joseph’s plan requires a chain of trustworthy appointees under a chief administrator.

verses.bibleText: And let them gather all the food of those good years that come, and lay up corn under the hand of Pharaoh, and let them keep food in the cities.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Joseph continues: “let them gather all the food of those good years that come, and lay up corn under the hand of Pharaoh, and let them keep food in the cities.” Three practical details stand out. The grain is to be gathered during the good years. It is to be held “under the hand of Pharaoh,” that is, under royal authority, so that it is protected from theft and private hoarding. And it is to be stored “in the cities,” close to where people live and can be supplied.

The phrase “under the hand of Pharaoh” shows Joseph’s tact once more. He is careful to place the entire scheme under the king’s control. Yet it also had real wisdom. Grain held centrally could be rationed fairly in the years of famine; grain scattered among private owners could be sold at ruinous prices or wasted. Storing it in many cities, each with the produce of its own district (v. 48), meant that relief would not depend on a single location that might be cut off.

The principle of putting resources under responsible stewardship runs through Scripture. Jesus praised the “faithful and wise steward, whom his lord shall make ruler over his household, to give them their portion of meat in due season” (Luke 12:42). Joseph will be exactly that steward for Egypt.

Joseph also says, “let them keep food in the cities.” The verb is shamar, to guard or watch over, the same word used when God placed Adam in the garden “to dress it and to keep it” (2:15). Stored grain had to be protected from damp, vermin, and theft for years at a time. Faithful stewardship includes the unglamorous work of guarding what has already been gathered.

wordNotes.term: בָּר (bar) — corn
wordNotes.explanation: Bar is threshed, clean grain, ready for storage and use. It is used again in Genesis 41:49 and throughout the famine story (42:3, 25; 45:23). Proverbs warns that the one who withholds grain in time of need will be cursed, but blessing comes on the one who sells it (Proverbs 11:26), which fits Joseph’s later distribution.

verses.bibleText: And that food shall be for store to the land against the seven years of famine, which shall be in the land of Egypt; that the land perish not through the famine.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Joseph states the purpose of the plan: “that food shall be for store to the land against the seven years of famine … that the land perish not through the famine.” The grain is not to be gathered for Pharaoh’s wealth or prestige but as a reserve held in trust for the land. Its whole point is preserving life.

The word “perish” is literally “be cut off.” Joseph pictures a nation wiped out by hunger, its people dying and its life coming to an end. Against that prospect, the reserve will stand as a guarantee that Egypt survives. Later Joseph will tell his brothers that God sent him ahead “to preserve life” and “to save your lives by a great deliverance” (45:5, 7). The plan he lays before Pharaoh is the earthly means by which that divine purpose is carried out.

In this single counsel Joseph combines faith and planning without tension. He believes God has determined the famine; he also believes God has given time and means to meet it. He neither presumes on a miracle nor relies on human cleverness alone. The God who warned Pharaoh also enabled Joseph to devise a plan, and the result would be life for many.

The reserve would serve more than Egypt. When the famine reached Canaan, the grain laid up under Joseph’s hand would feed Jacob and his sons, the family through whom God had promised to bless the world (42:1-2). Paul later applied the lesson of shared provision to the churches: “your abundance may be a supply for their want,” so that there may be equality (2 Corinthians 8:14). Plenty saved wisely becomes the means of meeting other people’s need.

wordNotes.term: פִּקָּדוֹן (piqqadon) — store
wordNotes.explanation: Piqqadon, from paqad, means something deposited and kept in trust. It is used of goods entrusted to a neighbour for safekeeping (Leviticus 6:2, 4). The grain is pictured as a deposit held on behalf of the land until it is needed, not as Pharaoh’s private treasure.

wordNotes.term: וְלֹא־תִכָּרֵת הָאָרֶץ (velo’-tikkaret ha’arets) — that the land perish not
wordNotes.explanation: Karat means to cut, and in the passive “to be cut off,” to perish. God promised after the flood that all flesh would never again be “cut off” by waters (Genesis 9:11). Here the same verb pictures a land destroyed by hunger. Joseph’s plan, under God, keeps Egypt from being cut off.

verses.bibleText: And the thing was good in the eyes of Pharaoh, and in the eyes of all his servants.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the thing was good in the eyes of Pharaoh, and in the eyes of all his servants.” The court accepts both the interpretation and the plan. There is no record of debate, no counter-proposal from the magicians who had failed, no jealousy voiced against the foreign prisoner. The whole assembly sees the wisdom of what Joseph has said.

The phrase “good in the eyes of” recalls earlier moments in Joseph’s story, where he found favour in the eyes of Potiphar and of the prison keeper (39:4, 21). The Lord had given him favour then, and he does so now on a far larger stage. The same God who turned the heart of a jailer turns the heart of a king. God can make even an enemy “to be at peace with him” (Proverbs 16:7).

The agreement of “all his servants” also matters for what follows. Joseph is about to be raised over officials who had served Pharaoh for years. Their consent to the plan prepares the way for their acceptance of the man.

wordNotes.term: וַיִּיטַב הַדָּבָר בְּעֵינֵי (vayyitav haddavar be‘eney) — the thing was good in the eyes of
wordNotes.explanation: Yatav, to be good or pleasing, with “in the eyes of,” is a common Hebrew way of saying that something met with approval. It is used when Pharaoh’s court is pleased to hear of Joseph’s brothers (Genesis 45:16) and when a proposal pleases the people (Deuteronomy 1:23). Here it marks the acceptance of Joseph’s counsel.

verses.bibleText: And Pharaoh said unto his servants, Can we find such a one as this is, a man in whom the Spirit of God is?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Pharaoh turns to his servants with a question that expects no answer: “Can we find such a one as this is, a man in whom the Spirit of God is?” The point is that no one like Joseph could be found anywhere. Joseph had advised Pharaoh to look for a discerning and wise man, and Pharaoh realises that the man is standing in front of him.

What Pharaoh saw was not merely a clever administrator. He saw in Joseph a power beyond human ability: the capacity to reveal what God was about to do and to devise a plan equal to it. He attributes this to “the Spirit of God” (ruach ’elohim). How much the pagan king understood by those words is uncertain. Elohim can mean God or gods, and a polytheist might have meant “the spirit of the gods,” as Nebuchadnezzar later said of Daniel (Daniel 4:8). Yet Joseph had spoken of one God throughout, using singular verbs, and the narrator records Pharaoh’s words without correction because they are true. The reader of Genesis knows that the Spirit of God had moved upon the waters at creation (1:2), and that the same Spirit was at work in this man.

The Old Testament repeatedly shows the Spirit of God equipping people for particular tasks: Bezaleel for the craftsmanship of the tabernacle (Exodus 31:3), the elders for leadership with Moses (Numbers 11:17), Joshua for leading Israel (Numbers 27:18), and the coming Branch of Jesse, on whom “the spirit of wisdom and understanding” would rest (Isaiah 11:2). Joseph is the first person in Scripture of whom this is said. His gift is not ecstatic or spectacular but expressed in wisdom, insight, and sound judgement for the good of others.

It is fitting that the recognition comes from a foreign king. Joseph’s life had borne witness in every place he had lived. Potiphar saw that the Lord was with him (39:3), the prison keeper trusted him with everything, and now Pharaoh confesses that God’s Spirit dwells in him. Jesus said, “Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16). The Spirit who filled Joseph is promised to all who ask the Father (Luke 11:13), and his fruit is still seen most clearly in faithful character and service.
