wordNotes.term: רוּחַ אֱלֹהִים (ruach ’elohim) — the Spirit of God
wordNotes.explanation: The same phrase describes the Spirit moving upon the waters at creation (Genesis 1:2) and filling Bezaleel “in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge” (Exodus 31:3). Spoken by a pagan king, it may have meant “a divine spirit” or “the spirit of the gods” (compare Daniel 5:11, 14). Yet Joseph had pointed only to the one God, and Scripture presents the phrase as a true description of God’s gift to him.

wordNotes.term: הֲנִמְצָא כָזֶה (hanimtsa’ khazeh) — can we find such a one as this
wordNotes.explanation: A rhetorical question with the passive of matsa’, to find: “Could one like this be found?” The expected answer is no. Similar questions in Scripture highlight someone beyond comparison, such as the “virtuous woman” whose price is far above rubies (Proverbs 31:10) and Job, of whom God said “there is none like him in the earth” (Job 1:8).

verses.bibleText: And Pharaoh said unto Joseph, Forasmuch as God hath shewed thee all this, there is none so discreet and wise as thou art:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Pharaoh now addresses Joseph directly: “Forasmuch as God hath shewed thee all this, there is none so discreet and wise as thou art.” He repeats the exact words Joseph had used, “discreet and wise” (v. 33). Joseph had described the man Egypt needed; Pharaoh declares that Joseph is that man.

The reason Pharaoh gives is significant. He does not praise Joseph’s natural intelligence or his reading of dreams as a skill. He says, “God hath shewed thee.” Joseph’s repeated insistence that God was the source has been heard and accepted. A king who had heard Joseph say “It is not in me” (v. 16) now credits Joseph’s wisdom to God. The servant’s humility has brought honour to his Master.

The contrast with Egypt’s experts is complete. All the wise men of Egypt (v. 8) had been unable to explain the dream; now Pharaoh says that “there is none so discreet and wise” as this Hebrew. Paul observes that God makes foolish the wisdom of this world (1 Corinthians 1:20), and James teaches that true wisdom comes down from above (James 3:17). Joseph’s wisdom was of that kind, and even a pagan court could recognise it.

Joseph had not applied for the position. He had described the kind of man Egypt needed and left the choice with Pharaoh. Proverbs observes that “a man’s gift maketh room for him, and bringeth him before great men” (Proverbs 18:16), and that the one diligent in his work “shall stand before kings” (Proverbs 22:29). Joseph’s gift had been exercised faithfully in obscurity, and now God made room for it at the highest level.

wordNotes.term: אַחֲרֵי הוֹדִיעַ אֱלֹהִים אוֹתְךָ (’acharey hodia‘ ’elohim ’otekha) — forasmuch as God hath shewed thee
wordNotes.explanation: Hodia‘ is the causative of yada‘, to know: “God has caused you to know.” Pharaoh recognises that Joseph’s knowledge was given by God, not achieved. The same verb is used of God making known his ways to Moses (Psalm 103:7) and of Daniel thanking God, who “hast made known unto me” the king’s matter (Daniel 2:23, in Aramaic).

verses.bibleText: Thou shalt be over my house, and according unto thy word shall all my people be ruled: only in the throne will I be greater than thou.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Pharaoh announces Joseph’s appointment: “Thou shalt be over my house, and according unto thy word shall all my people be ruled: only in the throne will I be greater than thou.” Joseph is placed over the royal household and over the whole population. Only the throne itself remains above him.

The pattern of Joseph’s life now reaches its height. In Potiphar’s house he was placed over everything except his master’s wife (39:6, 9). In the prison he was placed over everything under the keeper (39:22). Now he is placed over everything in Egypt except the throne. Three times he has been given authority with a single reserved limit, and in Potiphar’s house he showed that he would respect such a limit even under great pressure. A man who could be trusted with one kind of boundary could be trusted with this one.

The phrase “according unto thy word shall all my people be ruled” is literally “upon your mouth all my people shall kiss.” Its exact meaning is debated. It may mean that the people will submit to his commands, perhaps by kissing in homage, or that they will be fed at his word, since one Egyptian idiom links kissing with eating. Either way, the whole nation will depend on what Joseph says.

The psalmist summarises the moment: the king “made him lord of his house, and ruler of all his substance: to bind his princes at his pleasure; and teach his senators wisdom” (Psalm 105:21-22). Stephen tells it the same way before the Sanhedrin (Acts 7:10). Joseph’s exaltation to the right hand of the throne becomes in Scripture a picture of how God raises the humble, and it anticipates the One to whom the Father has committed all authority (Matthew 28:18).

wordNotes.term: וְעַל־פִּיךָ יִשַּׁק כָּל־עַמִּי (ve‘al-pikha yishshaq kol-‘ammi) — according unto thy word shall all my people be ruled
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “and upon your mouth all my people shall kiss.” Nashaq usually means to kiss, and a kiss could express homage and submission (Psalm 2:12; 1 Samuel 10:1). The sense may be “all my people will do homage at your command.” Others connect the verb with a word for arming or ordering, or with an Egyptian idiom for being fed. Whatever the nuance, the whole people will be governed by Joseph’s word.

wordNotes.term: רַק הַכִּסֵּא (raq hakkisse’) — only in the throne
wordNotes.explanation: Kisse’ is a seat of honour and authority, the royal throne. The single limit recalls the one exception in Potiphar’s house (Genesis 39:9). Joseph later describes his office as “a father to Pharaoh, and lord of all his house” (Genesis 45:8). The throne remains Pharaoh’s; all else is Joseph’s to administer (compare Esther 10:3).

verses.bibleText: And Pharaoh said unto Joseph, See, I have set thee over all the land of Egypt.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Pharaoh said unto Joseph, See, I have set thee over all the land of Egypt.” This is the third time in four verses that Pharaoh speaks (vv. 38, 39, 41), and Joseph has not said a word in reply. He does not thank the king, negotiate terms, or protest his unworthiness. The silence fits the man who said “It is not in me.” He had not sought this honour and he does not grasp at it. Providence has arranged it, and he receives it.

The verb “I have set” is literally “I have given.” The same verb was used when the prison keeper “committed” all the prisoners into Joseph’s hand (39:22), and when the Lord “gave” him favour in the keeper’s sight (39:21). Pharaoh thinks he is giving Joseph authority, and he is. But behind the king’s gift stands the God who gives and takes away. Daniel would later tell Nebuchadnezzar that “the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will” (Daniel 4:17).

“Over all the land of Egypt” reflects a recognised Egyptian title for the highest official below the king. The phrase frames the installation ceremony: Pharaoh says it here, and the narrator repeats it in verse 43. Within a single day, the Hebrew slave has become the chief minister of the greatest nation on earth.

wordNotes.term: רְאֵה נָתַתִּי אֹתְךָ (re’eh natatti ’otekha) — See, I have set thee
wordNotes.explanation: Natan, to give or set, is a common but weighty verb. Pharaoh uses the perfect tense of a decree: “I hereby set you.” The narrative has used natan repeatedly of what was given to Joseph (Genesis 39:21-23). The psalmist reminds readers that promotion finally comes from God, who “putteth down one, and setteth up another” (Psalm 75:7).

verses.bibleText: And Pharaoh took off his ring from his hand, and put it upon Joseph's hand, and arrayed him in vestures of fine linen, and put a gold chain about his neck;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The investiture follows at once, and every item has meaning. “Pharaoh took off his ring from his hand, and put it upon Joseph’s hand.” The signet ring carried the royal seal; whoever wore it could stamp documents with the king’s own authority. Ahasuerus later gave his ring first to Haman and then to Mordecai with the same effect (Esther 3:10; 8:2). Joseph now speaks with Pharaoh’s voice.

Pharaoh “arrayed him in vestures of fine linen.” Egyptian linen was famous for its quality, and the finest grades were worn by royalty and priests. Joseph’s story could almost be told through his clothes: the special coat from his father, stripped by his brothers (37:3, 23); the garment left behind in Potiphar’s house (39:12); prison clothing exchanged for something fit for the court (v. 14); and now the linen of a ruler. Each change marks a turning point.

Finally Pharaoh “put a gold chain about his neck.” Egyptian reliefs show officials receiving broad gold collars from the king as a sign of honour. The neck that had known the iron of captivity now wears gold. The psalmist remembered that Joseph’s feet were hurt with fetters and he was “laid in iron” (Psalm 105:18). The same God who allowed the chains now gives the chain of honour. Daniel would receive similar honours in Babylon, clothed in scarlet with a gold chain about his neck (Daniel 5:29).

The reversal is complete, but it was never Joseph’s achievement. He had been faithful in a slave’s tunic and in prison rags. The fine linen was a gift. In the end of the Bible, the bride of the Lamb is granted to be arrayed in fine linen, clean and white (Revelation 19:8), clothing given by grace to those who were once in rags.

wordNotes.term: טַבַּעְתּוֹ (tabba‘to) — his ring
wordNotes.explanation: Tabba‘at is a signet ring, probably from a root meaning to sink or impress, since it was pressed into clay or wax to make a seal. It is used of the rings given to Haman and Mordecai (Esther 3:10; 8:2). Possession of the king’s signet meant authority to issue decrees in his name (Esther 8:8).

wordNotes.term: בִּגְדֵי־שֵׁשׁ … רְבִד הַזָּהָב (bigdey-shesh … revid hazzahav) — vestures of fine linen … a gold chain
wordNotes.explanation: Shesh, fine linen, is an Egyptian loanword, later used for the linen of the tabernacle and the priests’ garments (Exodus 26:1; 28:39). Revid, chain or collar, appears elsewhere only in Ezekiel’s picture of God adorning Jerusalem with jewellery, including “a chain on thy neck” (Ezekiel 16:11). Both items mark dignity bestowed by a superior.

verses.bibleText: And he made him to ride in the second chariot which he had; and they cried before him, Bow the knee: and he made him ruler over all the land of Egypt.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Pharaoh “made him to ride in the second chariot which he had.” Chariots were a mark of high rank in Egypt, and the second chariot after the king’s own belonged to the second man in the kingdom. Ordinary people walked; Joseph now rides through the streets in royal procession. The title “second” matches an Egyptian designation for the vizier.

Heralds ran ahead, and “they cried before him, Bow the knee.” The word they cried, ’avrekh, is not ordinary Hebrew, and its meaning has long been discussed. It may be an Egyptian word meaning “Attention!” or “Make way!” It sounds like the Hebrew word for kneeling, which is how the King James translators and older Jewish interpreters understood it. Either way, the cry announced that a man of supreme authority was passing and that all should give him honour.

The narrator closes the scene with “and he made him ruler over all the land of Egypt,” repeating the phrase of verse 41. Joseph’s brothers had mocked his dreams of rule: “Shalt thou indeed reign over us?” (37:8). Now all Egypt bows before him, and his brothers soon will too.

The New Testament presents a greater exaltation in similar terms. Because Christ humbled himself to the death of the cross, “God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name: that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow” (Philippians 2:9-10). Joseph was honoured as second to Pharaoh; Christ sits at the right hand of God, above every authority (Ephesians 1:20-21). The comparison should not be pressed beyond what Scripture gives, but the pattern is plain: the rejected one, lifted up by God, becomes the one before whom others bow and from whom they receive life.

wordNotes.term: אַבְרֵךְ (’avrekh) — Bow the knee
wordNotes.explanation: A unique word in the Old Testament. Its sound resembles the Hebrew barakh, to kneel, as in Psalm 95:6, “let us kneel before the LORD.” Many see it as an Egyptian loanword meaning “Attention!” or “Do homage!” The herald’s cry recalls the honour proclaimed before Mordecai (Esther 6:9, 11) and points ahead to the universal homage given to Christ (Philippians 2:10).

wordNotes.term: מִרְכֶּבֶת הַמִּשְׁנֶה (mirkevet hammishneh) — the second chariot
wordNotes.explanation: Mishneh means second, double, or next in rank. It is used of the second-ranking priest (2 Kings 23:4) and of Mordecai, who was “next unto king Ahasuerus” (Esther 10:3). Merkavah, chariot, became a sign of royal pomp (1 Samuel 8:11). The phrase marks Joseph as second only to Pharaoh.

verses.bibleText: And Pharaoh said unto Joseph, I am Pharaoh, and without thee shall no man lift up his hand or foot in all the land of Egypt.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Pharaoh seals the appointment with a solemn declaration: “I am Pharaoh, and without thee shall no man lift up his hand or foot in all the land of Egypt.” The words “I am Pharaoh” work like an oath or royal signature. The king invokes his own authority to guarantee what he grants. Later, when the Lord confronts another Pharaoh, he will declare “I am the LORD” again and again (Exodus 6:2, 6-8), and the contest of those two claims will run through the plagues.

“Lift up his hand or foot” is a vivid way of saying that nobody could do anything without Joseph’s permission. Every action in the kingdom, from the highest official to the field worker, now falls under his authority. Joseph, who had been unable to move beyond a prison wall, now controls the movement of a nation.

Yet Joseph’s authority remains delegated. It rests on Pharaoh’s word and ultimately on God’s purpose. He will use it, not for revenge on those who wronged him or for his own enrichment, but for the preservation of life. Jesus later taught that greatness in his kingdom means serving others (Mark 10:42-45). Joseph’s use of power, though set in an ancient court, shows that same spirit of service.

The king’s “I am Pharaoh” stands in quiet contrast with Joseph’s first words in the chapter, “It is not in me” (v. 16). Pharaoh grounds authority in himself; Joseph grounds every gift in God. The man who disclaimed all power of his own is the one to whom all power in Egypt is handed. Jesus taught the same reversal: “whosoever shall humble himself shall be exalted” (Matthew 23:12).

wordNotes.term: לֹא־יָרִים אִישׁ אֶת־יָדוֹ וְאֶת־רַגְלוֹ (lo’-yarim ’ish ’et-yado ve’et-raglo) — shall no man lift up his hand or foot
wordNotes.explanation: A Hebrew idiom for total control: no action, whether with hand or foot, could take place without Joseph’s consent. Hand and foot together cover the whole range of human activity. The phrase is the reverse of Joseph’s own earlier condition, when his feet were hurt with fetters (Psalm 105:18), and it matches the psalmist’s summary that he was given power “to bind his princes at his pleasure” (Psalm 105:22).

verses.bibleText: And Pharaoh called Joseph's name Zaphnath-paaneah; and he gave him to wife Asenath the daughter of Poti-pherah priest of On. And Joseph went out over all the land of Egypt.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Pharaoh completes Joseph’s new identity with a name and a marriage. “Pharaoh called Joseph’s name Zaphnath-paaneah.” Renaming was an act of authority; only a superior could give a name, as Nebuchadnezzar renamed Daniel and his friends (Daniel 1:7). The new name marked Joseph as an Egyptian official and made him acceptable at court. Its meaning is uncertain. The most widely held view takes it as Egyptian for “God speaks and he lives” or “the god has said he will live,” a fitting description of the man through whom God spoke to save lives. Other suggestions link it to food and life. Whatever its exact sense, the Hebrew narrator continues to call him Joseph.

Pharaoh also “gave him to wife Asenath the daughter of Poti-pherah priest of On.” On, called Heliopolis by the Greeks, lay near modern Cairo and was the chief centre of the worship of the sun god Ra. Its high priest held one of the most honoured offices in Egypt. Asenath’s name probably means “she belongs to Neith,” an Egyptian goddess, and her father’s name means “he whom Ra has given.” Joseph is thereby joined to one of the noblest families in the land.

The marriage raises a natural question, since Abraham and Isaac had taken care that their sons should not marry Canaanite women (24:3; 28:1). The text records Joseph’s marriage without comment or censure. It was arranged by Pharaoh, and Joseph was hardly in a position to refuse. What follows suggests that Joseph did not adopt his father-in-law’s religion. He gave his sons Hebrew names that praise the God of his fathers (vv. 51-52), and those sons were later received by Jacob as heads of tribes in Israel (48:5). Like Daniel in Babylon, Joseph accepted a foreign name and a place in a foreign court without accepting foreign gods.

“And Joseph went out over all the land of Egypt.” The new vizier began his work at once.

wordNotes.term: צָפְנַת פַּעְנֵחַ (tsafnat pa‘neach) — Zaphnath-paaneah
wordNotes.explanation: An Egyptian name rendered into Hebrew letters. The most common reconstruction reads it as “God speaks and he lives,” though other readings have been proposed, and the Septuagint and later Jewish tradition offered guesses such as “revealer of secrets.” Like the Babylonian names given to Daniel and his friends (Daniel 1:7), it marked Joseph’s place in a foreign court without changing his allegiance (Genesis 45:3).

wordNotes.term: אֹן (’on) — On
wordNotes.explanation: An Egyptian city whose name means “pillar,” probably referring to the obelisks of its sun temple. The Greeks called it Heliopolis, “city of the sun.” Jeremiah calls it Beth-shemesh, “house of the sun,” and predicts the breaking of its images (Jeremiah 43:13). Ezekiel names it Aven, a play on a Hebrew word for wickedness (Ezekiel 30:17).

verses.bibleText: And Joseph was thirty years old when he stood before Pharaoh king of Egypt. And Joseph went out from the presence of Pharaoh, and went throughout all the land of Egypt.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The narrator pauses to give Joseph’s age: “Joseph was thirty years old when he stood before Pharaoh king of Egypt.” He had been seventeen when his brothers sold him (37:2). Thirteen years had passed, years of slavery in Potiphar’s house and confinement in the king’s prison. Those years were not wasted. In them Joseph learned the language and customs of Egypt, gained experience managing a household and a prison, and above all was proved in faith and character. “The word of the LORD tried him” (Psalm 105:19).

“Stood before Pharaoh” is an expression for entering a king’s service. David was thirty when he began to reign (2 Samuel 5:4). Jesus was about thirty when he began his public ministry (Luke 3:23), after years of hidden preparation in Nazareth. The parallel is a matter of the age at which God brought each into public service, not a hidden code, but it fits the wider pattern of patient preparation before a work of deliverance.

“And Joseph went out from the presence of Pharaoh, and went throughout all the land of Egypt.” He did not settle into the comforts of the palace. He travelled the whole country, presumably to survey its fields and cities, appoint the officers his plan required (v. 34), and prepare storage before the first good harvest came in. His promotion became immediate labour. The man who had served faithfully when no one noticed now served diligently when everyone was watching.

wordNotes.term: בְּעָמְדוֹ לִפְנֵי פַּרְעֹה (be‘omdo lifney par‘oh) — when he stood before Pharaoh
wordNotes.explanation: To “stand before” a king means to serve him as an official or attendant. David “stood before” Saul in his service (1 Samuel 16:21), and Daniel and his friends were chosen to “stand in the king’s palace” (Daniel 1:4-5). Elijah used the same idiom of serving God: “the LORD God of Israel, before whom I stand” (1 Kings 17:1).

verses.bibleText: And in the seven plenteous years the earth brought forth by handfuls.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The first half of the prophecy comes true: “in the seven plenteous years the earth brought forth by handfuls.” The phrase pictures the reaper grasping stalks so heavy with grain that each handful is a rich yield, or perhaps that the harvest came in bundles. The earth responds to its Creator’s word just as Joseph had said it would.

The brevity of the verse is significant. One line records seven years. The years of plenty, which Pharaoh might once have treated as the main point of a good dream, pass almost without comment. What matters is what is done with them. The next two verses describe Joseph’s work, and that work, not the abundance itself, becomes the focus.

The fulfilment also confirms Joseph as a true messenger of God. A prophet’s word is tested by whether it comes to pass (Deuteronomy 18:22), and the first seven years give Egypt a long demonstration that Joseph spoke truly. When the famine arrives, no one will doubt that it too was foreseen. The psalmist sings of the God who visits the earth and waters it, crowning the year with his goodness (Psalm 65:9-11). Egypt’s full barns were his gift long before they were Joseph’s achievement.

God could have given seven ordinary harvests before the famine. Instead he gave years so rich that a fifth could be stored without strain. The abundance was itself part of his provision for the coming need. Paul writes that “God is able to make all grace abound toward you; that ye, always having all sufficiency in all things, may abound to every good work” (2 Corinthians 9:8). God often supplies more than enough in one season so that his people can serve in the next.

wordNotes.term: לִקְמָצִים (liqmatsim) — by handfuls
wordNotes.explanation: Qomets is a handful, the amount a closed hand can hold. The priest took “his handful” of the grain offering to burn on the altar (Leviticus 2:2; 6:15). In the plural with this preposition the sense is “in handfuls” or “abundantly,” describing ears so full that each handful yields a rich return (compare Psalm 72:16).

verses.bibleText: And he gathered up all the food of the seven years, which were in the land of Egypt, and laid up the food in the cities: the food of the field, which was round about every city, laid he up in the same.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Joseph puts his plan into practice: “he gathered up all the food of the seven years … and laid up the food in the cities: the food of the field, which was round about every city, laid he up in the same.” The grain is collected systematically, year after year, and stored locally. Each city keeps the produce of its own surrounding fields.

The arrangement was wise in several ways. It avoided the cost and risk of transporting vast quantities of grain to a single centre. It kept supplies close to the people who would need them. It spread the risk, so that if one granary failed through fire, flood, or vermin, others remained. And it allowed local officers, the ones Joseph had recommended appointing (v. 34), to manage stores they knew. Egyptian records describe great royal granaries and officials responsible for them, and Joseph’s office resembles the role of an overseer of the granaries of the whole land.

The verse shows the patient side of Joseph’s character. Gathering grain for seven years required persistence when there was no visible crisis. Many would have questioned why so much should be stored when harvests were overflowing. Joseph’s diligence through those years reflects the faithfulness that marked him as a slave and as a prisoner. Jesus said, “He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much” (Luke 16:10). Joseph had been faithful with Potiphar’s house and with the prisoners; now he is faithful with a nation’s bread.

wordNotes.term: וַיִּקְבֹּץ (vayyiqbots) — and he gathered up
wordNotes.explanation: Qavats means to gather or collect, whether things or people. Joseph used it in his counsel, “let them gather all the food” (Genesis 41:35). The same verb describes God gathering his scattered people (Deuteronomy 30:3; Isaiah 40:11). In Egypt it describes the steady collection of grain over seven years.

verses.bibleText: And Joseph gathered corn as the sand of the sea, very much, until he left numbering; for it was without number.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The results were staggering: “Joseph gathered corn as the sand of the sea, very much, until he left numbering; for it was without number.” The quantity grew so large that the scribes stopped recording it. Egyptian officials were meticulous record-keepers, and the image of them abandoning their tallies conveys a harvest beyond calculation.

The comparison “as the sand of the sea” carries special weight in Genesis. God promised Abraham that his seed would be “as the sand which is upon the sea shore” (22:17), and Jacob reminded God of that promise when he feared Esau (32:12). The phrase belongs to the language of covenant blessing. Here it is applied to grain, but the echo is deliberate. The blessing God promised to Abraham’s family is flowing through Abraham’s great-grandson to Egypt and, soon, to the nations.

The abundance also prepares for the next verses. Joseph’s fruitfulness in grain is immediately followed by his fruitfulness in sons (vv. 50-52). The God who multiplies the harvest is the same God who builds families, and both are signs of his blessing in a land of exile.

wordNotes.term: כְּחוֹל הַיָּם (kechol hayyam) — as the sand of the sea
wordNotes.explanation: Chol, sand, with the sea, is the Old Testament’s standard image for a number too large to count. It describes Abraham’s promised descendants (Genesis 22:17; 32:12), Israel in Solomon’s day (1 Kings 4:20), and Solomon’s breadth of understanding (1 Kings 4:29). Its use for Joseph’s grain ties the harvest to the covenant blessing.

wordNotes.term: חָדַל לִסְפֹּר (chadal lispor) — he left numbering
wordNotes.explanation: Chadal means to cease or stop; safar means to count, the root behind the word for a scribe (sofer). The idea of stores beyond counting recalls God’s challenge to Abram to “tell the stars, if thou be able to number them” (Genesis 15:5). The scribes gave up because the amount exceeded their means of recording (compare Genesis 16:10).

verses.bibleText: And unto Joseph were born two sons before the years of famine came, which Asenath the daughter of Poti-pherah priest of On bare unto him.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Between the years of plenty and the years of famine, the narrator pauses to record a family event: “unto Joseph were born two sons before the years of famine came, which Asenath the daughter of Poti-pherah priest of On bare unto him.” The placement is deliberate. The birth of the sons stands at the centre of the closing section, between the gathering of grain (vv. 47-49) and the arrival of famine (vv. 53-57).

The timing matters. The sons were born “before the years of famine came,” in the season of blessing. Joseph’s personal life shared the fruitfulness of the land. For a man who had been torn from his family at seventeen and had spent his young adulthood in slavery and prison, the gift of a wife and children was itself a restoration. God had not only raised him to power; he had given him a home.

The repeated mention of Asenath’s father, “priest of On,” reminds the reader that Joseph’s household was set in the heart of Egyptian society. That makes what follows more striking. In naming his sons, Joseph will speak not of Egypt’s gods but of the God of his fathers. The Egyptian setting does not determine the faith of the home. Joseph’s sons would later be adopted by Jacob as his own (48:5), so that two tribes of Israel came from this marriage.

wordNotes.term: בְּטֶרֶם תָּבוֹא שְׁנַת הָרָעָב (beterem tavo’ shenat hara‘av) — before the years of famine came
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “before the year of the famine came.” Terem, before, often marks events God arranges ahead of need, as when Rebekah came out to the well “before” the servant finished praying (Genesis 24:15) and when God promises, “before they call, I will answer” (Isaiah 65:24). Joseph’s sons arrive within the season of plenty.

verses.bibleText: And Joseph called the name of the firstborn Manasseh: For God, said he, hath made me forget all my toil, and all my father's house.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Joseph called the name of the firstborn Manasseh: For God, said he, hath made me forget all my toil, and all my father’s house.” The name Manasseh sounds like the Hebrew for “making to forget.” Joseph gives his son a Hebrew name, not an Egyptian one, and builds it around a confession of what God has done.

What has God made him forget? “All my toil,” the hardship and trouble of thirteen years, and “all my father’s house,” which probably refers to the pain associated with his family: the hatred of his brothers, the pit, the sale, the long separation. The two phrases may form a single idea, “all my trouble connected with my father’s house.” Joseph is not saying that he no longer cares for his father or has wiped his family from his memory. The following chapters show how much he still remembers them: he weeps when he hears his brothers speak of their guilt (42:24), asks anxiously whether his father is alive (43:27; 45:3), and longs to see Benjamin. Forgetting here means that the pain no longer rules him. God has given him so much joy that the old wounds have lost their power to embitter.

There is an irony in naming a child “forgetting,” for every time Joseph called his son, he would be reminded of what God had healed. The name keeps the memory of suffering alive while declaring that God has overcome it. Isaiah uses the same language for God’s promise to his people: “thou shalt forget the shame of thy youth” (Isaiah 54:4). Joseph does not deny his past; he remembers it within the larger story of God’s grace.

Why did Joseph, now ruler of Egypt, not send word to his father at once? The text does not say. He may have been unwilling to expose his brothers’ crime to their father, or he may have waited for God to open the way, trusting the dreams God had given him. The narrator does not criticise him, and his later conduct shows no lack of love. The healing that Manasseh’s name records also prepared Joseph to forgive when the moment came (45:5; 50:19-21).

wordNotes.term: מְנַשֶּׁה … נַשַּׁנִי (menashsheh … nashshani) — Manasseh … hath made me forget
wordNotes.explanation: Menashsheh is formed from nashah, to forget, in an intensive form: “one who causes to forget.” Nashshani is “he has made me forget.” The naming follows the pattern of Leah’s and Rachel’s sons, each named with a confession about God (Genesis 29:32-35; 30:6). Similar language appears in God’s promise that former troubles will be forgotten (Isaiah 65:16).

wordNotes.term: עֲמָלִי (‘amali) — my toil
wordNotes.explanation: ‘Amal means labour, but especially wearisome toil and trouble. It is used of Israel’s affliction in Egypt (Deuteronomy 26:7) and of the Servant who “shall see of the travail (‘amal) of his soul, and shall be satisfied” (Isaiah 53:11). Joseph’s toil was not only physical work but the misery of slavery and injustice.

verses.bibleText: And the name of the second called he Ephraim: For God hath caused me to be fruitful in the land of my affliction.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the name of the second called he Ephraim: For God hath caused me to be fruitful in the land of my affliction.” Ephraim sounds like the Hebrew for “double fruitfulness” or “fruitful.” If Manasseh looks back to the pain God has healed, Ephraim looks around at the blessing God has given.

The word “fruitful” reaches back to the beginning of Genesis. God blessed humankind and said, “Be fruitful, and multiply” (1:28). He promised Abraham, “I will make thee exceeding fruitful” (17:6), and Isaac blessed Jacob that God would make him fruitful (28:3). Joseph sees in his second son a share in that covenant blessing. Jacob would later bless Joseph as “a fruitful bough, even a fruitful bough by a well; whose branches run over the wall” (49:22).

Yet Joseph calls Egypt “the land of my affliction.” For all his power, wealth, and family, Egypt is not home. The word “affliction” is the same one God would use of Israel’s oppression in Egypt centuries later: “I have surely seen the affliction of my people which are in Egypt” (Exodus 3:7). Joseph’s experience anticipates the nation’s. God did not remove Joseph from the place of suffering; he made him fruitful within it. Later the same God would multiply Israel in Egypt even under oppression (Exodus 1:7, 12), and then bring them out.

That is a word for all of God’s people who live in places they would not have chosen. Paul wrote from prison that his chains had furthered the gospel (Philippians 1:12). Jesus taught that a grain of wheat bears much fruit only after it falls into the ground and dies (John 12:24). Fruitfulness in affliction is a recurring work of grace. Joseph’s two sons together tell the story: God heals the past and blesses the present, while the land of promise still lies ahead (50:24-25).

wordNotes.term: אֶפְרָיִם … הִפְרַנִי (’efrayim … hifrani) — Ephraim … hath caused me to be fruitful
wordNotes.explanation: ’Efrayim is related to parah, to bear fruit, and its form may suggest “doubly fruitful.” Hifrani is the causative, “he has made me fruitful,” the same verb God used in blessing Abraham (Genesis 17:6) and Jacob (Genesis 28:3; 35:11). Ephraim’s name declares that the covenant promise of fruitfulness was being fulfilled even in Egypt.

wordNotes.term: בְּאֶרֶץ עָנְיִי (be’erets ‘onyi) — in the land of my affliction
wordNotes.explanation: ‘Oni means affliction, misery, or oppression. God saw Hagar’s affliction (Genesis 16:11, a related form) and Leah’s (29:32). He would later see “the affliction of my people which are in Egypt” (Exodus 3:7). Joseph’s phrase foreshadows Israel’s bondage and God’s faithfulness to those who suffer there.

verses.bibleText: And the seven years of plenteousness, that was in the land of Egypt, were ended.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the seven years of plenteousness, that was in the land of Egypt, were ended.” A single sentence closes the good years. The verb means “came to an end” or “were completed,” and it marks the boundary Joseph had foretold. Seven years exactly, just as the dream had shown.

The brevity reminds the reader how quickly times of abundance pass. For seven years Egypt had more than it could use. Many must have assumed the good seasons would continue, as people usually do when life is easy. But the prophecy had set a limit, and the limit arrived. Scripture often warns against assuming that present prosperity will last. Jesus told of a rich farmer who planned bigger barns and said to himself, “Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years,” only to hear, “Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee” (Luke 12:19-20). Joseph’s barns were different: they were filled for the sake of others, with the end of the plenty in view.

The verse is a quiet hinge. It ends the account of what Joseph did with the time given to him, and it opens the time in which that preparation will be tested.

wordNotes.term: וַתִּכְלֶינָה (vattikhleynah) — were ended
wordNotes.explanation: From kalah, to be completed or come to an end. The same verb, in another form, described the famine that would “consume” the land (Genesis 41:30). It is used of God finishing creation (Genesis 2:1-2) and of the water spent in Hagar’s bottle (21:15). The good years reached their appointed end exactly as God had said.

verses.bibleText: And the seven years of dearth began to come, according as Joseph had said: and the dearth was in all lands; but in all the land of Egypt there was bread.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the seven years of dearth began to come, according as Joseph had said.” The narrator explicitly ties the event to Joseph’s word. What Joseph had spoken from God came to pass in its second half as surely as in its first. The phrase “according as Joseph had said” confirms him once more as a reliable spokesman of God’s purposes.

Two statements follow, set in sharp contrast: “the dearth was in all lands; but in all the land of Egypt there was bread.” The famine was not confined to Egypt. Canaan and other surrounding regions suffered too, which was unusual, since Egypt’s river depended on rains far to the south while Canaan depended on local rain. Yet in the middle of a hungry world, one land had bread, and it had bread because God had warned and Joseph had prepared.

The contrast is not only between Egypt and other countries but between foresight and the lack of it. The nations around had experienced the same years of plenty but had made no special provision. Joseph’s plan made the difference between life and death for multitudes. Proverbs observes that “the wise shall inherit glory: but shame shall be the promotion of fools” (Proverbs 3:35). The detail also sets the stage for the next chapter. Among the hungry lands was Canaan, where Jacob and his sons lived. The famine that brought Egypt to Joseph’s storehouses would soon bring Joseph’s family to his feet.

wordNotes.term: כַּאֲשֶׁר אָמַר יוֹסֵף (ka’asher ’amar yosef) — according as Joseph had said
wordNotes.explanation: The same formula of fulfilment used of God’s word, “as he had said,” describes the birth of Isaac (Genesis 21:1) and the fulfilment of prophecy throughout Scripture (1 Kings 15:29). Applied to Joseph, it confirms that his interpretation was God’s own word. The phrase recalls the cupbearer’s testimony, “as he interpreted to us, so it was” (Genesis 41:13).

wordNotes.term: לֶחֶם (lechem) — bread
wordNotes.explanation: Lechem means bread, and more broadly food of any kind. Its presence or absence runs through the famine story (Genesis 41:55; 43:31; 47:13-19). Later God would give his people bread from heaven in the wilderness (Exodus 16:4), and Jesus would declare, “I am the bread of life” (John 6:35).

verses.bibleText: And when all the land of Egypt was famished, the people cried to Pharaoh for bread: and Pharaoh said unto all the Egyptians, Go unto Joseph; what he saith to you, do.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
As the famine deepened, the Egyptians began to feel it: “when all the land of Egypt was famished, the people cried to Pharaoh for bread.” Their own private stores ran out first. Perhaps they had saved little, trusting that the good years would continue, or perhaps the length of the famine simply exhausted what they had. Either way they turned to the king, who stood in their eyes as the guarantor of the land’s welfare.

Pharaoh’s answer is brief and complete: “Go unto Joseph; what he saith to you, do.” The king does not try to manage the crisis himself. He sends his people to the man God had raised up and commands them to obey him. This shows how fully Pharaoh had entrusted his authority to Joseph, and how much confidence the seven years had given him. The famine was going exactly as predicted, and the only man who had foreseen it was the only man who could meet it.

Pharaoh’s words find a striking echo in the Gospel of John. At the wedding in Cana, when the wine ran out, Mary said to the servants, “Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it” (John 2:5). The resemblance in wording is close, and in both scenes people in need are directed to the one who can supply it, with the instruction to obey his word. The New Testament does not draw the parallel explicitly, and it should be handled with restraint. Yet the pattern is unmistakable: God’s appointed provider stands ready, and the needy are told to go to him. Jesus himself said, “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden” (Matthew 11:28), and “he that cometh to me shall never hunger” (John 6:35).

wordNotes.term: לְכוּ אֶל־יוֹסֵף (lekhu ’el-yosef) — Go unto Joseph
wordNotes.explanation: A simple imperative: “Go to Joseph.” It directs the whole nation to the one man who holds the bread. The command “what he saith to you, do” uses the ordinary verbs ’amar, to say, and ‘asah, to do, linking Joseph’s word to obedience. The Septuagint wording is very close to Mary’s instruction at Cana (John 2:5), and the call to come to the one who gives food recurs in Isaiah 55:1.

verses.bibleText: And the famine was over all the face of the earth: And Joseph opened all the storehouses, and sold unto the Egyptians; and the famine waxed sore in the land of Egypt.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the famine was over all the face of the earth.” The phrase is broad, describing the whole known world of the ancient Near East as far as the narrative is concerned. The expression “all the face of the earth” recalls the language of the flood narrative and the scattering at Babel (7:3; 11:9), and it reminds the reader that God’s purposes in Joseph reach beyond one nation.

“And Joseph opened all the storehouses, and sold unto the Egyptians.” The grain gathered over seven years is now released. Joseph sold it rather than giving it away. That policy had good reasons. The grain had been collected as a tax and belonged to the crown; selling it encouraged careful use of a supply that had to last seven years; and it allowed the reserve to serve foreigners as well. Proverbs pronounces a blessing on the one who sells grain in time of need, while condemning the one who withholds it to drive up the price (Proverbs 11:26). Joseph neither hoarded nor squandered.

“And the famine waxed sore in the land of Egypt.” Even with the storehouses open, the famine grew more severe. Joseph’s plan did not make the hardship disappear; it made survival possible. Chapter 47 will show the later stages of the famine, when the Egyptians exchanged money, livestock, and land for food. Here the emphasis falls on the beginning of relief: the doors of the storehouses opened, and life was preserved.

Joseph handled enormous wealth at a time of desperate need, a situation that has corrupted many officials. Egyptian tomb inscriptions show nobles boasting that they fed the hungry in years of want; Joseph’s record is told without boasting, and when the money came in he brought it into Pharaoh’s house (47:14), not his own. The man who refused Potiphar’s wife because his master had trusted him with everything shows the same integrity over a nation’s bread.

wordNotes.term: וַיִּשְׁבֹּר (vayyishbor) — and sold
wordNotes.explanation: Shavar usually means to break, but a related verb from the noun shever, grain, means to buy or sell grain. Joseph “sold grain” to the Egyptians; in chapter 42 his brothers come “to buy corn” with the same root (Genesis 42:2-3). Amos condemns merchants eager to sell grain with false measures (Amos 8:5-6), the opposite of Joseph’s just stewardship.

wordNotes.term: עַל כָּל־פְּנֵי הָאָרֶץ (‘al kol-peney ha’arets) — over all the face of the earth
wordNotes.explanation: A phrase for the whole land surface, used of the flood’s reach (Genesis 7:3; 8:9) and the scattering of nations from Babel (11:8-9). Its scope depends on context; here it means all the lands within the horizon of the story, from Egypt to Canaan and beyond. The phrase highlights that Joseph’s storehouses served the wider world.

verses.bibleText: And all countries came into Egypt to Joseph for to buy corn; because that the famine was so sore in all lands.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The chapter closes with a panoramic view: “all countries came into Egypt to Joseph for to buy corn; because that the famine was so sore in all lands.” People from many nations make the journey to Egypt, and the narrator says they came “to Joseph.” The Hebrew slave, once sold to traders on their way to Egypt, now receives traders from every land who come to him for life.

This is the first great fulfilment of God’s promise to Abraham: “in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed” (12:3). Through one descendant of Abraham, raised up by God in a foreign land, the nations around are kept alive. Joseph did not choose this role; he was carried into it through betrayal, slavery, false accusation, and forgotten years. Later he would explain to his brothers, “God did send me before you to preserve life” and “to save much people alive” (45:5; 50:20).

The verse also turns the story back toward Canaan. Among “all countries” is the land where Jacob lives with his sons. The next chapter opens with Jacob hearing that there is corn in Egypt (42:1). Joseph’s dreams of sheaves bowing to his sheaf are about to be fulfilled, not through Joseph’s seeking but through the hunger that drives his brothers to the storehouses he controls.

In the larger story of Scripture, the scene foreshadows a still greater gathering. The world in its spiritual famine is invited to come to Christ, who was rejected by his own, exalted by God, and made the source of life for all who come to him. The prophets foresaw nations streaming to the Lord (Isaiah 2:2-3), and the Revelation pictures a great multitude from every nation, kindred, people, and tongue, who “shall hunger no more” (Revelation 7:9, 16).

wordNotes.term: וְכָל־הָאָרֶץ בָּאוּ מִצְרַיְמָה (vekhol-ha’arets ba’u mitsraymah) — and all countries came into Egypt
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “all the earth came to Egypt.” Ha’arets, the earth or land, stands for its inhabitants, as in “the whole earth was of one language” (Genesis 11:1). The phrase matches the worldwide reach of God’s pledge to bless every family on earth through Abraham’s seed (Genesis 12:3; 22:18).

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: What does it look like to wait for God when the people who could help you have forgotten you?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: The God who rules the Nile and the seasons remembered Joseph at the right time, spoke through him to a pagan king, and raised him from the dungeon to rule so that many lives would be saved.
discussionQuestions: Why might God have allowed Joseph to wait two more years after the cupbearer’s release?
What does Joseph’s first word to Pharaoh, “It is not in me,” reveal about how he understood his gift?
How does Joseph combine confidence in what God has determined with careful human planning?
In what ways does Joseph’s path from prison to power anticipate Christ’s humiliation and exaltation, and where must the comparison stop?
What do the names Manasseh and Ephraim teach about how God heals past pain without erasing it?
commonMisunderstandings: Joseph did not possess a technique for reading dreams; he insisted the interpretation came from God.
Belief that God has determined the future did not make Joseph passive; the certainty of the famine was the reason to plan for it.
Joseph’s Egyptian name, dress, and marriage do not mean he abandoned the God of his fathers; he gave his sons Hebrew names that praise God.
“God hath made me forget” does not mean Joseph stopped caring for his family; the following chapters show how deeply he remembered them.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Keep God at the centre, as Joseph does in every speech: God gives the dream, God gives the meaning, God has fixed the event, and God makes Joseph fruitful. Joseph’s wisdom and his rise are gifts that serve the saving of life.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: If you feel forgotten in a place you did not choose, the God who remembered Joseph has not lost sight of you; trust his timing, give him the glory for every gift, and use the season you are in to serve others.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: God rules history and reveals the future through his chosen servants; the pattern of suffering before glory in Joseph’s life points to Christ, who humbled himself to death and was exalted as Lord and Saviour of the world.
flow: Pharaoh’s dreams showed that even the mightiest ruler cannot know or control the future without God.
Joseph gave God all the credit: the dream and its meaning came from heaven, and what God had fixed would surely happen.
The forgotten prisoner was raised to the right hand of the throne, and every knee bowed before him.
Christ, rejected by his own and condemned though innocent, has been exalted so that every knee shall bow and every tongue confess him Lord.
As the hungry world was told, “Go unto Joseph,” so all who hunger are invited to come to Jesus, the bread of life.
simpleIllustrations: A weather warning is not given to make people afraid but to give them time to prepare; God showed Pharaoh the famine so that lives could be saved.
A man who walks out of prison in the morning and into the palace by evening knows his promotion is not his own doing; Joseph’s first words before the throne said so.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you come to Jesus, the One God has exalted, and receive from him the bread that gives eternal life?
cautions: Do not promise that every faithful believer will be raised to wealth or power; Joseph’s exaltation served God’s saving purpose for many.
Do not allegorise every detail of the chapter; draw the link to Christ from the pattern of humiliation and exaltation that Scripture itself highlights.
Do not use the dreams to encourage seeking guidance through dreams or omens; Scripture is the sure word by which every claim is tested.

reflectionQuestions: Do I trust that God’s timing is right when my waiting seems longer than I can bear?
When others praise my abilities, do I point them to God as Joseph did?
How am I using the present season of plenty to prepare for leaner days, for myself and for others?
Has God made me fruitful in a place of affliction, and have I thanked him for it?
Do I see Christ’s path from the cross to the throne as the pattern for my own humility and hope?
